Retention and churn mitigation have consistently been central issues within business domains. This research addresses churn prediction in online gambling formally as a binary classification task. We propose solutioning this issue using a recurrent neural networks (RNN) driven approach. This methodology was tested using online gambling time-series data, which RNNs are well-suited to process efficiently. Performance evaluation of the models relied on standard metrics including accuracy, precision, and recall. Experiments demonstrated that for this specific context, selecting a particular architecture depends heavily on the priority assigned to specific metrics. Models built with n-BLSTM optimized for precision, those utilizing LSTM improved recall, and GRU-based models delivered superior accuracy and a balance between other relevant metrics. Furthermore, additional experiments revealed that training networks using exclusively recent historical time-series segments reduced the quality and reliability of results. We also analyzed the performance evolution of models trained at a specific instant $t$ when applied to future instances $t^{\prime}$. These results indicated that models trained at $t$ maintained adequate performance thereafter, implying that frequent retraining is unnecessary for high-frequency updates. However, performance exhibited noticeable variance caused by unique, one-off events that directly impacted the dataset.

The empirical outcomes align closely with simulations, demonstrating the functional doubling effect across ±2°.

This study introduces a strategy to reduce the volume of coupling matrix storage in volume-to-surface integral equation (VSIE) formulations, which are integral to analyzing electromagnetic interactions in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), particularly between the antenna and the body. We established that these interactions function as separate events among distant 3D elements when expressed in tensor formats, allowing decomposition via the Tucker model. This approach synergizes with adaptive cross approximation to efficiently solve complex VSIE issues. We proved that compressing the coupling matrix overcomes memory limitations associated with standard VSIE matrices by facilitating the utilization of GPU acceleration for matrix-vectors operations; this speed is essential for conducting numerical MRI simulations at clinical resolution times and voxel sizes. Specifically, our method enables GPU-computed calculations, taking approximately 33 seconds, to render MRI coils operating within a $1$ cm$^3/-$scale body model composed of $1$ mm³ elements. This feat was achieved by compressing the coupling matrix from roughly $80$ TB to about $43$ MB.

Empirical analysis shows the model surpasses other neural network-based medical image compression methods, achieving significantly higher PSNR scores (by ~35% and ~36% depending on interpretation), together with substantial improvements (~30-) in MS-SSIM and Color-SSIM. Instance segmentation involves delineating every individual object of focus within an image. Current state-of-the-art methodologies attain this objective through either refining detected object coarse estimates or partitioning semantic segmentation maps. In this study, we propose an original strategy known as object layering; this technique distributes numerous, even overlapping, objects across separate visual layers. By clustering spatially distant objects into a shared layer, individual instances become easily isolated through the extraction of connected components within each group. Distinct from prior techniques, our method eliminates hindered accuracy caused by complex morphological structures or significant occlusions between objects. With only minimal requirement for processing at later stages, our approach generates highly competitive performance metrics across varied test sets, including *C. elegans* image sets (BBBC), overlapping cervical cells (OCC), and in culture-derived images from cell line DNA damage (CCDB). Blockchain technology has garnered growing interest across diverse sectors such as supply chains, healthcare, and cryptocurrencies, yet it is hampered by poor scalability issues like high latency and low transaction throughput. To address these limitations, various solutions have emerged; sharding is one of the most promising among them. This approach falls into two primary types—Sharding-based Proof-of-Work (PoW) and Sharding-based Proof-of-Stake (PoS)—both of which offer high throughput with reasonable latency, though they introduce distinct security challenges. This study focuses specifically on analyzing the security of Sharding-based Proof-of-Stake (PoS) protocols. We evaluate their robustness by computing the probability of faulty block commits and quantifying the system's security through a calculation of "years to fail." Furthermore, numerical analysis is performed to verify and evaluate the efficacy of the proposed model.

This paper investigates the stochastic optimization of Areas Under Precision-Recall Curves (AUPRC), a technique essential for handling imbalanced classification problems. Existing literature has suggested several AUPRC optimization methods, yet few offer a stochastic framework with convergence guarantees, with current state-of-the-art iteration complexities capped at $O(1/\epsilon^5)$. We address these gaps by (i) introducing novel stochastic momentum approaches achieving a superior complexity of $O(1/\epsilon^4)$ and (ii) creating a family of stochastic adaptive methods sharing this complexity but exhibiting faster empirical convergence. To accomplish this, we introduce two critical techniques: randomly updating the tracking estimators for individual ranking scores in a coordinate-specific manner, and applying momentum updates to the stochastic gradient estimator used for tracking the objective's gradient. A key contribution involves a novel analysis of Adam-style processes. Comprehensive experiments across diverse datasets confirm the efficacy of these algorithms. Moreover, our proposed stochastic momentum and adaptive solvers independently contribute to solving two-level stochastic dependent compositional optimization problems.

Statisticians frequently navigate a decision between employing probability models and minimizing a loss function as an algorithmic paradigm. While both strategies are beneficial, and appropriate probabilistic tools can select the most suitable loss or model when the objective permits proper probabilization to explain data nature, the guidance breaks down if the chosen results in an improper probability model. Our study fills this gap by merging Hyvärinen's score—which targets infinitesimally small relative probabilities—with general Bayesian inference to create a cohesive decision-making framework for both improper models and specific losses. Introducing the Hyvärinen (H) score as this unified selection criterion, we demonstrate its consistent ability to identify, under Fisher's divergence metric, the model—regardless of whether it is proper or improper—that best aligns with the data-generating process. Additionally, we prove that the corresponding H-posterior accurately recovers optimal loss function hyperparameters, including the difficult temperature parameters in generalized Bayesian inference, a capability exemplified in scenarios of model instability. Applying this approach to challenges like robust regression and non-parametric density estimation, we show cases where standard selection fails because the associated standard proper distributions yield from these losses but the true model lies outside them. These examples highlight improvements in the robustness-efficiency balance for these tasks and culminating a Bayesian application for KDE, establishing fresh methodology for stochastic calculus in this area.

The climate acts as a non-equilibrium system driven constantly by the interplay of dissipation and forcing. Spatial variations in solar radiation absorption provoke dynamic responses across all climate components, leading toward an approximate steady state or attractor; nevertheless, particular forcings and boundary conditions may support the coexistence of multiple such states. This study utilizes the Thermodynamic Diagnostic Tool (ThermDia) to examine the statistical features of five stable climates within an MITgcm model—an Earth configuration ranging from a completely frozen snowball to a thawed aquaplanet. Our goal was to assess the model's multistability by illustrating distinctive signs among these competing equilibrium scenarios, specifically concerning zonal heat and fresh-water transport patterns, the Lorenz energy cycles, and the rates of material entropy production, while analyzing sensitivity across different configurations. This analysis focused notably on adjusting cloud albedo representations and refining energy budget closures to observe how these attractors shift even when the modeled dynamics stay fixed, demonstrating that internal state variables are altered nevertheless. Metrics from Thermo-DIAG successfully quantify these variations, establishing the tool as a robust instrument for model validation.

The analysis examines the absence of significant signals in searches for heavy resonances (specifically ZZ or ZV decays) and axion-like particles (ALPs) causing nonresonant ZZ or ZH generation. These investigations target event states comprising two charged leptons originating from Z decays alongside two jets from Z, W, or Higgs decays, with sensitivity extending to resonance masses from 450 to 2000 GeV to account for whether bosons appear resolved or reconstructed as merged. The study leveraged proton-proton collision data from the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider recorded between 2016 and 2018, characterized by a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and a cumulative luminosity of $138 \text{ fb}^{-1}$. While no deviations from standard model predictions were detected, the results provide exclusion criteria in models such as the heavy extra-dimensional triplet scenario for bulk gravitons and $Z'$ ($W'$), as well as cross-section bounds for spin-1 and spin-1 resonant events across different masses. Furthermore, limits were established for ALP-mediated diboson production and ALP couplings within the frameworks of effective linear and chiral field theories. Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RISs) are considered a promising technology to shape the landscape of future wireless communication, yet their lack of processing ability combined with augmented channel complexity creates significant hurdles, notably the high pilot resource consumption required for channel estimation. Previous works have mitigated these issues by modifying RIS hardware structures or leveraging the mathematical nature of RIS channels to limit pilot requirements proportional to the number of elements, but such approaches still suffer from inherent dimension dependency. This paper introduces a dimension-free method for acquiring Channel State Information (CSI). Unlike conventional techniques that sequence transmissions between the Base Station (BS) and users in distinct time slots, we introduce a simultaneous signal transmission strategy during the CSI acquisition phase. Concurrent signals between the BS and user generate an Electromagnetic Interference Random Field (IRF) on the RIS, which necessitates the development of a specialized sensing IS architecture to analyze these characteristics accordingly. Further enhancing this system, we present three estimation algorithms; for one specific vM-EM algorithm, we utilize the fixed-point perturbation method to determine its asymptotic performance bound. Additionally, we derive both the Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB) and an asymptotic formula that characterizes the theoretical optimal performance of these estimators. Finally, simulation studies demonstrate that our concurrent signal approach and accompanying algorithms successfully achieve beamforming using dimension-independent CSI acquisition.

In an effort to curb pollutant emissions, bicycling is experiencing a resurgence, especially within cities; however, fatalities among cyclists have not exhibited a corresponding decline compared to other road users. Consequently, tracking cyclists is becoming vital to improving urban safety by enabling planners to create less hazardous routes. This work introduces a fully image-based framework designed to evaluate route risk from the cyclist’s viewpoint. By processing smartphone photo sequences, this generic system automatically detects specific events using multiple risk parameters derived from both cyclist movement and spatial analysis. Relying entirely on visual inputs allows the method to provide situational context independent of the cyclist’s technical skill level. Building upon this foundation with enhancements to a pre-existing mobile platform capable of capturing both imagery and video, sensor data was leveraged to automatically isolate bike-specific route segments utilizing behavior analysis techniques. Validated against real-world datasets, the approaches demonstrated promising efficacy in risk classification across distinct metrics and behavior identification accuracy.

This paper presents a hybrid solution combining a regularized zero-forcing transmit precoding (RZF-TPC) strategy with an adaptive coding and modulation (ACM) approach tuned by distance, designed specifically for aeronautical communication. The proposed RZF-TPC and distance-based ACM system adjusts its operating mode dynamically based on the range between the communicating aircraft. We establish an asymptotic, closed-form signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) expression for RZF-TPC within an aeronautical Rician channel, which utilizes a non-centered matrix dominated by line-of-sight propagation and accounts for realistic channel estimation errors and co-channel interference. Additionally, we derive an analytical formula to determine the optimal regularization parameter by minimizing the average mean-squared detection error. The design metric for our scheme is the achievable throughput, calculated via an asymptotic approximations based SINR. Monte-Carlo simulations confirm these theoretical findings and explore the influence of critical system parameters in detail; notably, the simulation outcomes align almost perfectly with theory. Specific simulations involving two aircraft traveling at standard cruising speeds (920 km/h) towards opposite ends of a 740 km course within an estimated 24-minute window confirm that our system, utilizing 64 transmission and 4 receiving antennas, successfully transmits 77 GB of data. Throughput is substantially superior compared to a previously investigated benchmark that employed eigen-beamforming transmit precoding alongside distance-based ACM in similar conditions.

Phase-separating systems driven away from equilibrium with chemical reactions exhibit two distinct mechanisms for violating time-reversal symmetry (TRS). The dominant source of such violation arises when conservative (non-reacting) and non-conservative sectors are governed by incompatible free energies; in the presence of both, the resulting structure aligns with 'Model AB.' A secondary, though fundamentally important, mechanism involves the breakdown of TRS within diffusive dynamics directly. This occurs at higher orders in the gradient expansion—if one ignores reactions but considers finite-order scaling—and characterizes 'Active Model B+' (AMB+). These mechanisms typically drive microphase separation via independent, diverging pathways, but this work introduces 'Model AB+,', unifying both forces simultaneously. Under conditions of slow reactions, the system manifests a unique hierarchical mode of microphase separation: a continuum of fluid 1 harboring large fluid 2 domains that incessantly generate, contain within them small fluid 1 droplets—which are swiftly dissolved back into the surrounding matrix—and sustain a "bubbly microphase separation regime" where conservative dynamics shape small-scale features within nonconservative reaction-driven larger architectures.

Procedure cloning addresses the limitations of standard imitation learning by moving beyond simple supervised input-output matching. While typical approaches learn directly from logged expert observations, this view is insufficient when demonstrations are derived from complex expert procedures like planning or search. In such domains—ranging from navigation and robotic manipulation to strategy games—the intermediate calculations reveal crucial logic that guides the output action, offering deep insight into the state-acting mapping. Our method, procedure cloning, utilizes supervised sequence prediction to mimic these internal expert computations. This allows the agent to learn not only "what" to do but "how and why" an action is determined, effectively internalizing expert strategies without requiring the simulation or specific tools necessary to perform them in real-time. Empirical results across game, robot, and navigation tasks demonstrate that preserving and imitating this computational reasoning capability enables policies with strong generalization, succeeding even in environments where direct application of the original expert's optimization procedure is impossible.

As machine learning becomes increasingly integrated into our society, it is essential to clearly understand both its advantages and limitations to ensure responsible deployment. Current ML evaluation platforms like board games or video titles provide established progress markers; however, because these constituent tasks remain intricate, it is often ambiguous which specific attributes drive overall difficulty for algorithms. Similarly, absent a comprehensive analysis of task properties, establishing significant links between disparate benchmark performances becomes exceedingly difficult. To address these gaps, we present a new environment offering a broad spectrum of ML problems and enabling the exact scrutiny of task component impacts. Called the Game of Hidden Rules (GOHR), we operationalize this approach through "board-clearing" mechanical challenges featuring a robust rule specification language. Our platform includes a captive, installable server capable of running these tasks locally. We outline specific rule-learning experiments within this system and aim to provide an active leader-board to encourage researchers attempting to master these rules. Distinctively, GOHR augments current tools by allowing targeted adjustments, empowering experimenters to determine precisely how every dimension of an agent's learning problem contributes to real-time algorithmic difficulty on demand.

Mobile Crowdsourcing Services (MCS) provide a rapid, low-cost method for scaling data collection, applicable across numerous sectors. Existing research indicates that systems like Foursquare (a location-based service) and Waze (a navigation tool) are susceptible to varied data poisoning attacks, a threat posed significantly by the ability to inject malformed inputs to deceive users. Yet, no comprehensive analysis has previously examined the scope and exploitability of Input Improper Validation (IIV) vulnerabilities within diverse MCS domains. To address this, the study leverages mobile app interfaces as attack vectors to develop a bespoke toolset and methodology, forming an end-to-end, feedback-driven analysis framework. Utilizing the MCS survey of ten popular services across five sectors previously unstudied, the researchers employed the proposed framework to transmit ten thousands of automatically constructed API inputs, thereby profiling the extent of the IIV attack surface. Shocking results reveal that eight out of ten examined services face severe IIV flaws capable of mass data poisoning. These flaws permitted adversaries to generate 7,400 deceptive API requests successfully fabricating dangerous online posts involving robberies and gunfire; furthermore, the vulnerabilities enabled the fabrication of implausible fitness feats, such as running supernatural speeds and covering impossible distances. The authors conclude by outlining implementable and scalable mitigation tactics that can substantially shrink the exposure to IIV attacks, emphasizing these measures as essential steps toward building trustworthy MCS environments.

Current astronomical data offer unparalleled insight into the physical characteristics and stellar populations of nearby galaxies, yet they only depict a present moment. In contrast, cosmological simulations illuminate the historical evolution that galaxies have undergone. By standardizing simulations to match current observable conditions, researchers can align historical events with modern galactic properties. This project emulates data from MaNGA, the premier integral field spectroscopic survey covering 10,000 diverse nearby galaxies, using the TNG50 cosmological run to create the MaNGIA (Mapping Nearby Galaxies with IllustrisTNG Astrophysics) mock dataset. By selecting TNG galaxies that mimic MaNGA's selection criteria, potential sampling biases are minimized. Datacubes resembling MaNGA observations were generated from all simulated galaxies and processed using the pyPipe3D tool to derive high-resolution stellar maps. This manuscript outlines these generation methods and presents preliminary analyses. The stellar demographics and motion patterns in the MaNGIA sample show broad concordance with actual observations. While specific discrepancies emerge—particularly regarding age and metallicity gradients in galaxies of intermediate mass and the structural motions within the massive stellar giants—these warrant deeper study. The findings extend prior efforts that produced analogous datasets of smaller scale. The final comprehensive dataset, comprising over 10,000 post-processed MaNGA datacubes analyzed via pyPipe3D and the specialized codes utilized to produce the mock samples, accompanied the public availability of a future publication.

We propose a quantum architecture linking mechanical nodes and magnonic nodes through optical channels. Cavity magnonics has advanced rapidly in recent years, leveraging collective spin excitations within ferrimagnetic crystals like yttrium iron garnet (YIG). These spin-based systems are viewed as promising constituents for future quantum networks, though their utility is constrained by intrinsic losses in magnon coherence—generally limited to around 1 µs in YIG. Herein, we demonstrate that coupling a magnonic system with a mechanical one via optical pulses enables the transfer and long-lived storage of arbitrary magnonic states (both classical and quantum) in a remote resonator. The fidelity of this transfer is contingent upon specific pulse parameters and channel loss. Furthermore, we establish that magnonic and mechanical nodes can be engineered into macroscopically entangled states. These findings validate quantum state transfer and entanglement dissemination within this new hybrid magnonic-mechanical network. Our work illustrates a viable pathway to bridge the fields of optomagnonics and optomechanics, facilitating the construction of long-distance quantum networks built upon mechanical and magnonic infrastructure.

Camera and LiDAR are two essential sensors for autonomous driving's 3D perception. The LiDAR captures precise 3D shapes and object locations, whereas cameras deliver abundant semantic features like color and texture. Combining these modalities has been proven to substantially elevate the performance of perception models by complementing each other's strengths. Nevertheless, existing datasets are often derived from specialized, high-cost data-capture vehicles; consequently, they cannot fully represent the nuances of realistic data distributions. To address this gap, we have assembled real-world instances featuring noisy distributions to build a robustness benchmark toolkit. This toolkit enables the systematic simulation of these challenging cases on conventional clean autonomous driving datasets. We validated the effectiveness of our tool by creating robustness benchmarks for nuScenes and Waymo, marking the first holistic, state-of-the-art evaluation of fusion methods to date. Key findings include: (i) fusion models typically fail under LiDAR disturbances, even when trained solely on such datasets; and (ii) gains from enhancing camera inputs pale in comparison to improvements from modifying LiDAR inputs. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient training strategy to bolster robustness. The toolkit, benchmark results, and associated code can be retrieved at https://github.com/kcyu2014/lidar-camera-robust-benchmark.

These findings are analyzed in the context of interpreting event-horizon scale observations from the GRAVITY telescope and the Event Horizon Telescope targeting Sgr A* and M87.

In the realm of medical image analysis, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) often face challenges caused by acquisition-related distribution mismatches between training and testing datasets. To address this, a Test-Time-Adaptation (TTA) approach has emerged recently. By optimizing the CNN individually for each incoming test image, TTA offers a robust, resource-efficient solution that improves resistance to shifts in data distribution without requiring cross-institutional data sharing or extra annotations. Historically, TTA methods have relied on auxiliary helper networks to align test-image features or predictions with those from the training phase; however, these helpers are frequently vulnerable to similar shifts themselves and may need task customization, which imposes limitations. To circumvent these issues, we present a novel TTA strategy based on matching feature distributions using a Field-of-Experts (FoE) model to align test inputs with those from training data. Within our FoE framework, we define the "experts" based on the univariate marginals derived from the feature maps of the primary task CNN. Furthermore, we augment this by calculating the Principal Components derived from local CNN features and using the resulting distribution of PCA coefficients as additional experts. The efficacy of our proposed FoE-driven method was validated across several MRI segmentation benchmarks—including four healthy tissue segmentation tasks across different anatomical regions and a lesion segmentation task in one anatomical region, all utilizing data from seventeen clinics—and one MRI registration challenge based on data from three clinics. Our findings demonstrate that while this method remains generally applicable to various tasks, it notably surpasses all previous TTA approaches specifically in lesion segmentation. regarding healthy tissue segmentation, our method outperforms generic, task-agnostic alternatives, although purpose-specific TTA methods still yield the best overall performance across many datasets. Stellar activity hinders the detection and characterization of exoplanets by introducing noise that can mask true planetary signals, a particular challenge for highly active M dwarfs which are key targets in the hunt for habitable worlds. To mitigate this and reach the sensitivity needed to find small planets, effectively managing activity-induced jitter is essential. This study evaluates the effect of choosing specific line lists for least-squares deconvolution on reducing dispersion in radial velocity datasets using optical data from the active M dwarf EV Lac, gathered via ESPaDOnS and NARVAL instruments. Two selection methodologies were compared: a parametric method utilizing line properties and a randomized algorithm capable of exploring the space of line combinations. A randomized approach was specifically refined to isolate activity signals from other noises, with tests conducted on ADLeo and DS Leo across different activity scenarios to ensure reliability. Planet-injection simulations supported the findings. Results indicate that parametric selection achieves a radial velocity RMStreduction of less than 10%, whereas the randomised strategy delivers a consistent improvement exceeding 50\% across all activity levels studied. If activity remains the primary noise factor, this method enables the creation of line lists rich in activity-sensitive indicators, facilitating more robust determination of stellar rotation periods by better isolating rotation modulation in the processed data. Furthermore, utilizing these derived line lists successfully retrieves synthetic signals (0.3-0.6 \($$\text{M\_\text{Jup}}$$\text{)} in 10-day orbits even under moderate ($20\text{ m/s}$) to intense ($200\text{ m/s}$) activity conditions, with no significant distortion of the actual planetary signal.

Deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) individuals depend heavily on captions during live television broadcasts, which are currently assessed using standardized regulatory metrics. However, these existing metrics fail to account for DHH users' actual preferences and does not capture the perceived meaningfulness of specific captions. To address this limitation, it is necessary to develop evaluation measures that consider the relative significance of words within a transcript. We conducted an analysis examining correlations between two distinct types of word embeddings and human-annotated scores reflecting word importance, drawing from existing language corpora. Our results show that normalized contextual embeddings generated by BERT demonstrate a stronger correlation with manually labeled importance data compared to word2vec-based embeddings. We now provide access to paired datasets containing both word embeddings and human-verified importance ratings. Furthermore, by training word importance classification models using these data, we successfully created a utility pilot achieving an F1-score of 0.57 on a six-class classification task.

To explore the possibility of forming heavy baryonium bound states consisting of a heavy baryon and its antiparticle, this work examines their interaction potential using heavy baryon perturbation theory. Furthermore, the potential's inherent uncertainties and their impact on the resulting heavy baryonium mass spectrum have been analyzed.

Mesh redistribution, which repositions a standard off-grid layout with higher concentrations in selected regions to prevent element distortion, can be modeled as a diffomorphic mapping problem between mass density functions. Diffeomorphisms remain highly valuable for moving meshes because they ensure geometric validity; notably, for exact mappings on a sphere, this process typically relies on Optimal Transport (OT), even handling the mapping from non-smooth to non-smooth density functions with exactness. However, the field has evolved with the introduction of optimal information transport (OIT), recent rigorous research which enables both exact and inexact diffomorphic mappings by streamlining the associated partial differential equations (PDEs) with the same precision as classical optimization.

This work provides the inaugural comparative analysis applying OT and OIT specifically to sphere-based adaptive mesh refinement. We detail strategies to extend these methods from spheres to broader manifold structures via novel generalizable computations. A significant contribution here involves employing provably convergent solvers; despite lacking boundary conditions or a standard comparison principle in the PDE setup rendering convergence generally unprovens, we achieve success with OIT. Results demonstrate that OIT outperforms OT in this context by offering superior numerical outcomes and easier adaptation to moving meshes. Consequently, for OT to emerge as a robust solution for such challenging scenarios, substantial advancements in its sphere-specific solver accuracy and a validated extension to other manifolds are required.

Recent research confirms that deep neural networks (DNNs) are susceptible to adversarial examples that cause incorrect predictions through the injection of subtle, barely noticeable perturbations. This work examines the transferability of such adversarial examples, a critical factor in real-world contexts where the target models' architecture or parameters remain hidden. Although numerous studies indicate that adversarial examples tend to overfit the surrogate models they were generated from—thereby diminishing the efficacy of transfer attacks against distinct targets—we propose a new approach to counter this overfitting known as Reverse Adversarial Perturbation (RAP). Unlike methods that minimize the loss for a solitary adversarial point, RAP generates adversarial examples situated within a region maintaining a uniform, low loss value by introducing a worst-case perturbation at every step of the optimization process. This strategy is framed as a min-max bi-level optimization problem. Integrating RAP into iterative attack procedures yields more robust adversarial examples that resist shifts in decision boundaries, effectively curbing surrogate model overfitting. Extensive comparative experiments illustrate a substantial enhancement in adversarial transferability achieved by our proposed approach. Moreover, RAP effectively merges with various existing black-box attack methods to further amplify transferability. Notably, experiments on a practical image recognition service, the Google Cloud Vision API, show a 22% improvement in targeted attack success rates compared to prior methods. Implementation details and source code are publicly accessible via our GitHub repository at https://github.com/SCLBD/Transfer_attack_RAP.

We propose a two-phased deep reinforcement learning algorithm designed for resolving demanding control tasks. Cell-to-cell variations fuel numerous biologically significant processes, including cell destiny decisions and resistance to chemotherapy. The role of metabolism, particularly involving mitochondria, is gaining recognition as a pivotal driver of these variations. Since most eukaryotic cells contain multiple copies of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) subject to sequence variation, intra-cell mitochondrial diversity can emerge; this, in turn, may generate inter-cell differences and contribute to cellular stochasticity. This review examines genetic and non-genetic origins of both intra-cell mitochondrial discrepancies (differences between organelles within the same cell) and inter-cell discrepancies (differences between what appear identical) alongside the connections between mitochondrial genetics and phenotypes. We address mtDNA copy number stability, the widespread occurrence of microscale mtDNA mutations within cells ('microheteroplasmy'), and evolving knowledge of macroscopic mtDNA mutations across a cellular population ('macroheteroplasmy'). Additionally, we explore how supercomplecxes, cristae architecture, pH levels, and cardiolipin interactions may amplify the genotype-phenotype link. The discussion extends to membrane potential, mitochondrial networks, and their influence on the mitochondrial genome. Furthermore, considering recent advances, we revisit mitochondria's role in dampening genotype-phenotype associations through compositional complementation. The variety of these sources of variability underscores the critical need for future research incorporating single-mitochondrial measures to better understand cellular heterogeneity and intrinsic biological "noise."

Although 3D hydrodynamic simulation suggests such atmospheric trails may exist for stars with violent winds, this marks only a limited number instance confirmed observationally at 10830 åtrometers; yet, it continues serving as our primary test subject due to having the peak transit flux depth and most stretched structure ever seen, making it highly relevant even today.

Elemental crystals made of manganese, tellurium, or selenium exhibit chiral properties, making it essential for crystallographic analysis to resolve two physically distinct enantiomeric variants in order to understand the impact of chirality variations on sample traits. Current methods for identifying machine-generated text predominantly rely on binary classifications distinguishing between human and machine text—a strategy that risks significant harm to authors if deployed by scientific publishers during manuscript review due to potential error and the legitimate use of assistive technologies like translation. Because these tools may be incorrectly flagged as fully machine-written under binary schemes, our research simulates this vulnerability by deploying state-of-the-art detectors from the DAMPap2 dataset on translated passages from SciELO, discovering that model performance degrades to random chance. Consequently, we constructed a framework for developing a dataset that enables nuanced, multi-facet labeling (distinguishing translation types, paraphrasing tools, etc.) rather than a simplistic machine-versus-human binary, resulting in SynSciPass. Re-training the DAMPap2 detector on the SynSciPass dataset demonstrated that specifying information sources makes detection models significantly more effective against domain shifts and allows it to identify the specific technologies used to generate text. However, our findings also lead us to conclude that existing datasets lack the comprehensive realism required for the real world; they do not sufficiently address the variety and novelty inherent to actual journal submissions (as scientific texts and complete documents change), the impact when used alongside manual writing, or completely unknown technological distributions present during manuscript submission.

Accurate polyp detection is vital for effective early cancer detection during gastrointestinal endoscopy. However, endoscopy videos present greater challenges than individual still frames, combining richer contextual data with significant complexity. The camera movement, unlike the typical fixed-camera setup with moving objects, causes substantial background fluctuations between frames, while severe intra-frame artifacts like tissue specular reflections and fluid motion drastically alter the quality of neighboring frames, complicating feature integration across a sequence for improved predictions. To resolve these challenges, we introduce the Spatial-Temporal Feature Transformation (STFT) framework. STFT addresses spatial inconsistencies caused by motion through proposal-guided deformable convolutions for feature alignment. On a temporal basis, it incorporates a channel-aware attention mechanism that simultaneously assesses adjacent frames for relational correlation to enable adaptive aggregation based on image quality. Extensive experiments show that STFT enhances the robustness of the still-image baseline FCOS on CVC-Clinic and ASUMayo datasets, yielding a F1-score improvement of 10.6% and 20.6% in polyp localization, while also surpassing current state-of-the-art video-based techniques by margins of 3.6% and 8.0% in their respective datasets. The implementation is accessible at \url{https://github.com/lingyunwu14/STFT}.

This study examines the thermodynamic aspects of a deformed Schwarzschild black hole using a non-commutative (NC) gauge theory of gravity, proposing a novel evaporation model. Initially, the ADM mass, Hawking temperature, and entropy of this NC deformed black hole are analyzed. Specifically, the theory eliminates the usual divergent behavior of the Hawking temperature and highlights temperature disparities between polar and equatorial regions, while simultaneously uncovering a new fundamental Planck-scale length ($\Theta \approx 2.257 \times 10^{-35}\,{\text{m}}$). As the black hole nears its endpoint, the NC term reveals a residual entropy, $\hat{S}_0$. Further investigation into heat capacity and Gibbs free energy illustrates how this non-commutative framework modifies thermodynamic stability and drives phase transitions. Additionally, the influence of pressure on stability and transitions within this NC spacetime is explored. The analysis indicates that non-commutative parameters function analogously to thermodynamic variables and leads to a conclusion of second-order phase transitions in NC Schwarzschild black holes.

Future generations of experimental efforts offer the unprecedented capability to examine neutrino flavor oscillation with extreme precision. In this work, we investigate a model where the dark matter constituting our current universe comprises both sterile neutrinos and an exceedingly lightweight dark matter constituent. Utilizing a 3+1 neutrino flavor oscillation framework, we analyze the impact such a dark matter composition would have on solar neutrino fluxes, energy spectra, and electron neutrino survival probabilities, specifically using the 3+1 model. Existing data from solar neutrino detectors, including Super-Kamiokande, the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory, and Borexino, enable us to determine a strict upper limit for the ratio of the mass ($m_\phi$) to the Fermi constant ($G_\phi$) of the lighter dark matter particle, constraining the ratio $G_\phi/m_\phi$ to remain below $10^{30}\, G_{\rm F}\, \rm{GeV}$ in accordance with observations; (Note: Assuming standard unit conversions, the exponent is treated as a strict bound in the original text). Furthermore, in regimes characterized by an extremely small Fermi constant, the magnitude of temporal variations must not exceed 3% to maintain consistency with present solar neutrino data concerning electron neutrinos from electron neutrinos. Additionally, we conclude that next-generation instruments like DARIN, capable of performing high-precision flux measurements across low energy regions, impose supplementary constraints that effectively complement limitations currently established by existing detection methods within the next-generation of experiments.

Considerable advances have emerged regarding supervised and unsupervised learning-based multi-view stereo (MVS) architectures. Integrating the strengths of these approaches, particularly in terms of depth completion and precision while simultaneously reducing reliance on costly annotated datasets, this study introduces the Semi-Supervised MVS problem defined by sparse depth supervision. However, substantial variation in scenarios/view configurations in MVS data often violates core premises of classic semi-supervised learning (Semi-SS) concerning shared data distributions between label groups for unlabeled and labeled tasks. Consequently, we introduce a specialized Semi-Supervised MVS architecture termed SE-MVS which handles both cases where standard semi-similarity assumptions hold. It utilizes Consistency Regularization for scenarios fitting this standard assumption and enforces consistency via KL D constraints between original and random augment versions, and introduces Style Consistency loss where standard semi-meta assumptions fail, as these data do not fully match distributions. This technique transfers the unlabeled input feature style into labels to diminish style variations, and models the output while simultaneously supervised by labels provided by generated variables based from unlabeled/label sources originally processed together during the training. Extensive evaluation on BlendedMVS/DATU/GIT-Net/Temples datasets demonstrates that proposed approaches outperform current self-unsupervised and supervised foundational methods under equal model backbone settings.

This study details experiments involving pulsed photoacoustically excited laser interactions with turbid polymer materials, aimed at assessing sound velocity and detecting bulk inhomogeneities. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this pattern improves sensitivity for identifying bulk defects. These capabilities support research into soft matter systems, which may include biological specimens. An experimental evaluation using Grilon(R®) under varied conditions illustrated the proposed limitations inherent to the methodology.

This distinguishes the work in contrast to the prevailing approaches for optimal chemotaxis controls, as exemplified by Guillén-González et al. (*Controlling*, 12).

We present the Scalable ZX-calculus (SZX-calculus), a formal yet concise graphical framework for designing and verifying quantum computations. By moving from individual wires to registers of qubits and enabling compact sub-diagrams through binary matrices, our extension significantly expands capability for modeling complex quantum dynamics. The article confirms the proof-theoretical validity (both soundness and completeness) of the SZX-calculus and illustrates these benefits with applications to graph states and quantum error correction.

An efficient exploration strategy in reinforcement learning leverages an agent's uncertainty regarding the optimal policy; this works well for near-optimal results in tabular environments but proves difficult in non-tabular scenarios involving function approximators where precise uncertainty quantification remains a significant hurdle. Addressing these challenges, we note that standard value estimates often exhibit bias and temporal inconsistency. Consequently, we propose a new method to assess uncertainty over value functions by creating a distribution of temporal differences. This exploration signal accounts for specific state-action transitions to filter out value uncertainties that are irrelevant compared to those in agent parameters. Since this uncertainty metric conditions on transitions, we cannot act directly upon it. Instead, we integrate this information as intrinsic reward, transforming exploration into a distinct learning problem driven by temporal differences. Our approach employs a specific exploration policy tasked with gathering data characterized by high uncertainty, thereby creating a smooth curriculum for the entire lifespan that asymptotically disappears when value estimates become perfectly accurate. Testing on rigorous exploration tasks within Deep Mind Robotics and Atari 2600 environments demonstrates that our proposed framework successfully supports both diverse and profound exploration.

We investigate few-shot open-set recognition (FSOR), aiming to develop systems that simultaneously adapt quickly to novel classes using limited labels and accurately reject unknown inputs. Conventional open-set techniques designed for large-scale datasets fail in this scenario due to scarce data. Current approaches try to calibrate few-shot closed-set classifiers to detect negative samples via thresholding, though manually tuning these thresholds is difficult since required sensitivity varies across tasks. To address this, our study introduces a task-adaptive negative concept for FSOR that incorporates the learning of rejection thresholds into the training phase. We do this by enriching few-shot closed-set classifiers with extra negative prototypes derived from the few-shot data. Harnessing correlations within these few-shot classes during prototype generation allows us to learn task-specific, dynamic rejection boundaries. Furthermore, we have adapted our approach to handle generalized few-shot open-set recognition (GFSOR), addressing classification challenges involving many-shot and few-shot classes alongside the exclusion of negative examples. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets demonstrate the efficacy of these methods on both problem frameworks.

Stream processing services, particularly those sensitive to latency and reliant on high bandwidth, are primary drivers of network traffic. Characterized by data streams consisting of continuous sequences of elements that must be processed nearly in real time, these services struggle when communication delays or network bottlenecks increase. Fog computing addresses this by integrating with cloud infrastructure to push computation to the network edge, effectively reducing congestion; however, the diverse heterogeneity inherent in this hybrid cloud-fog architecture creates significant deployment complexities. This work introduces the Cloud-DATA to Stream application matching (COD) framework, a two-sided stable model designed to deploy data streaming applications—defined here as workflows of processing microservices—as they navigate the heterogeneous resources available in both edge environments and fog clusters.

In our model, the resource continuum in fog and cloud networks are ordered by microservice processing duration, whereas the data streams themselves prioritize resources based on residual bandwidth capacity, establishing a many-to-many preference pairing to guide allocations toward optimal outcomes regarding peak latency and overall network load stability. We utilized algorithms for stable many-many matching, ensuring alignment with application performance optimization on one side while further optimizing resource efficiency and overall communication volume. With evaluations in use cases spanning real-world and synthetic networks supporting fog-cloud scenarios, we have shown a performance enhancement over comparative techniques of 44 to 27% in terms of stream reduction and 2 to 22% in minimized latencies.

We present two analytically tractable models to clarify dynamic effects arising in resonant light scattering from subwavelength particles. Our results demonstrate that steep variations in an incident pulse's envelope can trigger counterintuitive scattering dynamics driven by the interference of modes exhibiting disparate relaxation rates. To validate these models, we analyze the dynamic light scattering of an infinite circular $GaP$ cylinder by an incident pulse with a square-envelope carrier frequency positioned near constructive interference (the super-modes of Mie). Specifically observing the singular sharp changes that appear just after the leading and trailing edges of an incident pulse, we observe that sharp fluctuations in the scattered field arise as the carrier frequency crosses the resonances closest to destructive interference at submultipole modes. We detail how the singularity behavior manifests at specific frequencies and shapes of an incident pulse, showing the mechanism of sharp fluctuations in the scattered field and the resulting energy conservation in the particle for short-lived resonance conditions. These findings highlight the necessity of accounting for dynamic mode coupling in resonance treatments when analyzing localized light scattering phenomena, which could lead to a better design and optimization of nanostructured devices that offer ultrafast and spatial resolution for sensing and emission. To assess the reliability of our analytical models to predict physical findings, we perform a numerical evaluation that involves comparing our model solutions against numerical results of full time-dependent solutions based on Maxwell equations, which provides a quantitative check. Through these comparisons, we explicitly discuss the pros, cons of applying finite size scaling to predict localized light scattering phenomena, which could allow us better design and optims these devices to enhance their spectral sensitivity in the ultra-short timescales.

The cores of dense primordial black hole clusters form dynamic regions featuring numerous interaction types, some creating transient, gravitationally bound pairs while others result in single scattering events. Unlike binary mergers, the gravitational background spectrum from CHE is sensitive to redshift-dependent rate variations, a factor that could aid in distinguishing primordial black holes from astronomical populations. In contemporary software quality management, peer programming reviews and automated code tests frequently occur concurrently. This paper introduces an approach to derive potential proofs for a query based on a provided Answer Set Programming (ASP) rule set by employing an abduction process where the space of abducibles is automatically derived exclusively from input rules rather than manual definition. Given user-provided facts (which may be empty), our technique identifies any auxiliary facts required to validate a query and presents these supplementary additions, thereby removing the burden on users to explicitly enumerate the entire abducible universe. Additionally, we offer a method to construct a set of directed edges representing the justification graph for the target query. By utilizing forms of implicit term substitution, our technique can integrate user-provided facts to appropriately adapt the abductive results. While prior abduction research has largely relied on goal-driven methodologies—often resulting in non-declarative solver implementations—little attention has focused on implementing abduction within bottom-up solvers like Clingo for ASP. We present innovative ASP programs that operate directly within Clingo to produce both abductive solutions and directed edge sets without altering the core solving engine.

Positron Emission Tomography (PET), extensively used in clinical diagnostics and medical research, is a focal topic of this study, where we investigate the advantages of leveraging quantum entanglement within linear polarized positron annihilation photon pairs through a mix of simulation and experimental verification. This Quantum-entangled PET approach introduces novel strategies to overcome critical obstacles in emerging imaging technologies. To illustrate its promise, we introduce a streamlined technique that utilizes solely the entangled photon data inherent in PET events to effectively quantify and eliminate both scatter and random background sources in patient studies.

Our results demonstrate that, for a constant volumes, the column morphology evaporates more rapidly than both the isolated drop and the mixed configuration. Furthermore, we provide experimental proofs showing that introducing shear into the fiber network lowers their intersection angle. This adjustment promotes the formation of a column state and consequently accelerates the drying speed of volatile liquids placed on the network.

Deep neural networks offer robust frameworks for modeling data and the functions that map data to other characteristics, often purportedly achieving "super-human" results when inferring these input-output relationships. However, specific challenges arise in applications like inelastic neutron scattering—and in broader scientific contexts—such as scarce labeled experimental data, the absence of result uncertainty quantification, and the limited interpretability of these complex models. This study addresses all three challenges. Specifically, we trained a deep neural network on simulated data to discriminate between two magnetic exchange models in a half-doped manganite. We then applied recent deterministic uncertainty quantification techniques to generate classification error estimates, highlighting the necessity of including accurate instrument resolution in training data to ensure reliable predictions on real experiments. Finally, we utilized class activation maps to identify which spectral regions most critically influenced the network's classification outcomes.

Assessing feasibility and stability within ecological networks remains a central yet daunting challenge in theoretical ecology. Pioneering research by May (1972), complemented by modern applications of random matrix theory, reveals universal, emergent patterns governing stability and feasibility in these dynamics. Nevertheless, limited exploration has addressed how temporal delays, combined with population dynamics, influence the occurrence of these feasible and stable states. This study examines the implications of delay on Generalized Lotka-Volterra dynamics for interacting species within isolated ecological contexts. We first establish a straightforward analytical relationship between stability and feasibility in delay-free scenarios where intra-species interactions predominate. Subsequently, we demonstrate that augmenting time delays triggers a phase transition in population dynamics: shifting the system from a static equilibrium to a stable non-point attractor regime. We analytically determine the critical delay marking this transition, confirming its accuracy through numerical simulations that yield excellent convergence. Finally, we devise a stability metric applicable to non-equilibrium states and demonstrate that, within the oscillatory regime generated by delays, system stability rises proportionally with ecosystem diversity.

A unique feature is an inference-level "zooming" refinement technique that notably boosts segmentation accuracy, particularly for tiny parts. Evaluations show substantial performance gains: FLOAT achieves 2.0% improved mean Intersection-over-Union (mIOU) and 4.8% improved segmented quality (sqIOU) compared to state-of-the-art methods on Pascal-Part-58; similar gains are observed at the larger Pascal-Part-108 scale. By integrating smaller parts and previously overlooked attributes, we have created Pascal-Part-201, the most comprehensive and difficult variant of the benchmark. On this new dataset, FLOAT yields remarkable improvements of 8.6% for mIOU and 7.5% for sqIOU, proving its robustness against strong variation in objects and parts. All associated datasets and code can be accessed at floatseg.github.io.

This research broadens the analysis of such semiclassical dyon ensembles to the context of $SU(3)$ Yang-Mills theory. Specifically, our study demonstrates that interaction dynamics within this regime yield the theoretically expected deconfinement transition of first-order nature, a process examined across temperatures both below and above $T_c$, along with detailed scrutiny of topological susceptibility and ensemble correlations. Furthermore, we analyze dyon systems defined within a trace-deformed Yang-Mills framework; our conclusions highlight the capacity of this deformation to sustain a confined state, potentially preserving the topological character of observables at high temperature regimes compared to the deformed confinement dynamics.

This project analyzes the microscopic governing mechanisms of the interaction between local spin and charge fluctuations across correlated electron systems. We conduct a detailed examination of the generalized on-site electrical susceptibility using several fundamental many-body frameworks, including the Hubbard atom, the Anderson impurity model, and the general Hubbard model. Specifically, the reason for the considerable suppression of diagonal entries (in Matsubara frequency) against a background of modest off-diagonal growth remains clearly identified. The suppression inherent in diagonal terms is attributed to electron scattering occurring on local magnetic moments, indicating that these moments experience a more extended lifetime along with strengthened effective interaction strengths with electrons. The subtle but diffuse enhancement in off-diagonal terms, conversely, is chiefly attributed to multiboson scattering events. While the deep interweaving between spin and charge domains is moderated at the Kondo temperature due to the gradual weakening of the effective spin-fermion coupling for local magnetic fluctuations at low frequencies, the comprehensive study illuminates the exact manner in which physical data is conveyed between various scattering pathways within interacting systems, emphasizing the crucial function of such coupling in governing correlated electron dynamics within the regime where perturbation methods are no longer strictly valid.

Current distillation techniques often fail to leverage training data efficiently; therefore, we introduce an innovation that distills knowledge utilizing merely a subset of the data, offering superior data efficiency. To facilitate this, we adapt standard teacher training by integrating self-regulation: the model updates only those samples that were misclassified occurred during a backward pass or where its prediction lacks sufficient confidence. In contrast to traditional methods that involve all samples equally, these techniques limit sample participation by controlling their frequency within the self-regulated training phase. A sample's significance is measured specifically by how often it triggers parameter updates, and these values subsequently serve as weights when calculating loss for student learning in the distillation stage. Titled "significance-based distillation" (SIG-DIS), our approach introduces this specific weighting mechanich. To critically compare, we also devised two distinct distilling strategies where a regular student learns from either these SIG-DIS-trained models (utilizing their significance metrics, termed "significance-guided distillation") or a non-regulated teacher ("hybrid/regulated" variations). Evaluations across benchmark datasets confirm that SIG-DIS and the comparative methods achieve performance on par with other state-ofthe art knowledge distilling methods but require a considerably lower number of data points.

Owing to its efficiency in computing and storage space, hashing has become a staple in image retrieval systems. While deep unsupervised hashing methods have recently gained prominence thanks to their ability to circumvent the high cost of manual annotations by leveraging deep learning, they are not without flaws. Most existing approaches rely on pre-calculating a similarity matrix to define pairwise relationships within the feature space, subsequently using this fixed matrix to guide the hash learning process; however, they effectively treat most data pairs without distinction. This workflow suffers from two main limitations: first, the static nature of the pre-compiled similarity matrix prevents it from remaining connected to and informed by the dynamic learning process, thus failing to fully capture semantic structures; and second, meaningful data relationships are often overshadowed by the sheer volume of low-yield pairs. To bridge these gaps, we introduce a Deep Self-Adaptive Hashing (DSAH) framework designed to capture semantic cues through two key innovations: Adaptive Neighbor Discovery (AND) and Pairwise Information Content (PIC). Specifically, AND begins by constructing neighborhood-based similarity matrices which are then continuously refined during learning to deepens the investigation of underlying semantic structures. Simultaneously, the Pairwise Information Content (PIC) metrics evaluate the discriminative value of data pairs, assigning adaptive weights to prioritize interactions between more dissimilar items based on the assumption that such discrepancies hold greater hash-learning potential. Comprehensive experiments across various datasets validate the efficacy of these mechanisms in driving superior deep hashing performance.

It is generally believed that the diversity of goods in the global economy has increased during our lifetimes. However, verifying this claim directly is challenging due to the lack of complete annual data on every available product in an economic system. We address this research gap by analyzing publicly accessible product text descriptions from major American corporations spanning 1997 to 2017. While other indicators of economic performance suggest rising productivity over these years, our text-derived analytics reveal that the diversity within the output of large firms in the United States has consistently fallen over recent history. We observe this decline through diverse multi-metric product diversity assessments that utilize a binary, Boolean-based similarity score between the offerings of competing firm pairs. Building on the advanced firm-analysis model developed by Hoberg and Phillips and enhanced with two more refined variables, our approach consistently indicates a marked decrease in the variety of goods produced by significant U.S. firms. These empirical findings provide a robust foundation for defining and preliminarily investigating specific hypotheses regarding why such product diversity is dwindling.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has become a favored strategy for developing Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems in data-scarce environments. The findings from extensive analysis and experiments demonstrate the dependency of downstream low-resource ASR performance on the quality and quantity of the pre-training SSL data; specifically, performance correlates positively with both increased similarity to and the volume of the pre-training corpus. We anticipate that this study will aid the speech research community in constructing more robust systems and will direct future investigations toward optimizing generalization within SSL-driven pre-training paradigms.

Waveform physiological metrics play a crucial role in caring for critically ill patients in intensive care units, though such recordings are vulnerable to artefacts that must be eliminated prior to their reuse for clinical alerts or further analysis and research. Precise artefact elimination mitigates bias and uncertainty in clinical evaluations as well as minimizes the false-positive rates of ICU alarms, making it a pivotal element of effective patient care. Our study introduces **DeepClean**, a prototype self-supervised artefact detection system based on a convolutional variational autoencoder; it sidesteps the need for expensive manual annotation by relying only on readily accessible 'clean' data for training. Evaluating against a dataset of invasive arterial blood pressure, the algorithm successfully identifies artifacts within 10-second segments with approximately 90% accuracy, both sensitivity and specificity aside. Moreover, **DeepClean** pinpoints affected high-quality and low-quality sample regions with significant precision and far exceeds baseline Principal Component Analysis in terms of artefact identification and waveform restoration. Because **DeepClean** utilizes a generative model approach, the tool could additionally be used for the imputation of missing records.

Deep neural networks are frequently utilized for automating diagnostics on medical imagery, yet a critical practical challenge for clinicians is forecasting future disease trajectories. Existing prognostic approaches often rely heavily on domain expertise and prove difficult to deploy. To address this, we reframe disease trajectory forecasting as a one-to-many prediction task. Drawing inspiration from a two-stage clinical decision-making process involving a radiologist and a general practitioner, our method employs a dual-component framework based on transformer architectures. One transformer analyzes the imaging modalities while sharing information among components, whereas its partner leverages shared internal states alongside fused auxiliary clinical data. Furthermore, the temporal dynamics of disease progression are captured within the transformer states, enabling treatment via a novel multi-task classification loss. We demonstrate that our approach effectively predicts structural changes in knee osteoarthritis as well as Alzheimer's clinical status directly from raw multi-modal inputs. Results indicate our method exceeds existing state-of-the-art baselines in both performance and calibration—metrics essential for real-world applications—with a codebase openly available at https://github.com/Oulu-IMEDS/CLIMATv2.

This study introduces a new trajectory prediction and planning framework designed for robot navigation within challenging outdoor settings. The method leverages multimodal data from an RGB camera, 3D LiDAR, and an odometry sensor to train a model capable of estimating the likelihood of successful trajectory execution, despite the partial reliability of the multi-source inputs. Employing encoder networks, we transform high-dimensional sensory streams into compact feature vectors and organize them into a connected graph structure. These graphs are utilized by an attention-based Graph Neural Network (GNN) to predict trajectory success rates. Additionally, we assess image and point cloud data individually to determine sensor trustiness, thereby adjusting the feature graph weights before they enter the GNN. At runtime, our system employs multi-sensor data to evaluate the feasibility of locally planned paths to minimize the risk of collisions or failures. The framework exhibits resilient prediction performance even when one or more sensor modalities are compromised in complex real-world scenarios, validated through navigation experiments with a spot robot across various outdoor environments.

Empirical observations on nonlinear pricing indicate that consumers suffer from cognitive biases due to a limited grasp of complex price structures, notably treating perceived average prices as proxies for marginal ones. This perceptual error leads to suboptimal consumption decisions. Treating errors in marginal pricing as an exogenous variable, this paper determines the optimal quadratic price mechanisms for monopolists and a social welfaire-maximizing entity within a model featuring a continuous spectrum of consumers holding varied beliefs. Under simplified assumptions regarding preferences, costs, and consumer perceptions, the analysis finds that such biases do not alter the maximum attainable welfare, nor does it meaningfully impact the monopoly efficiency loss; consequently, these distortions are insufficiently potent to justify reforms aiming to improve public welfare through price transparency contrasts to that finding, these biases almost always increase monopolists' profits. Notably, the results highlight an intriguing scenario where small levels of bias simultaneously benefit both consumers and monopolists, implying that fully educating the public about true marginal prices does not constitute an invariably optimal social outcome: the document further clarifies that such biases can actually undermine the effectiveness of two-tier increasing tariffs as a mechanism for reducing total consumption.

While irreversible logic, including standard industry semiconductor circuits, consumes significant switching energy, reversible logic offers a path to reduced energy costs. Superconducting logic, utilizing flux quanta to represent bits, serves as an ideal platform for reversible operations that consume low energy compared to the magnitude of a single flux quantum. This study simulates ballistic reversible shift register gate designs powered strictly by input bits, introducing a novel storage loop. This innovation creates an asynchronous system capable of handling inputs arriving at varying times while maintaining strict ordering, where states—along with moving and stored bits—are encoded as flux polarity. The mechanism operates through elastic flux swapping between moving and stored components, evolving a concept traditionally used in prior irreversible superconducting shift registers. The base design (BSR) is a 1-in, 1-out gate; however, it is extensible. We demonstrate that sequencing two BSRs without adding power yields 2-bit memory and that a modified 2-in, 2-out BRS can set and route states based on input ports and exit routes; effectively, this establishes the first asynchronous reversible two-input 2 gate. Furthermore, a collective coordinate model was applied to analyze system dynamics, reducing the motion to two governed coordinates under potentials defined by input data and initial stored flux quanta.

Subsurface convection zones exist widely in early-type stars; although these thin layers, driven by opacity peaks, transfer negligible heat, they crucially influence stellar magnetic characteristics and variability. This study challenges the prior assumption that such zones are universally present. While standard 1D evolutionary models indicate conective instability, these models sometimes fail to account for the critical Rayleigh number required for actual convection inception. This reveals the presence of "stability windows" where no subsurface convection occurs, specifically at metallicity subsider solar levels. In stars resembling LMC metallicity, stable regions lie between $8M_\odot$ and $16M_\odot$, expanding to the range $[8M_\odot -35 M_\odot]$ for SMC metallicity. These intervals offer distinct targets for isolating the effects of subsurface convection against other origins of luminosity variability in massive stellar objects.

As Internet of Things (IoT) technologies advance, sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks must accommodate massive, sporadic device traffic via grant-free random access. Specifically, during each time slot, base stations (BS) rely on pilot sequences from active devices to perform Joint Activity Detection and Channel Estimation (JADCE). However, the combination of large-scale antenna arrays and dense device populations makes traditional JADCE methods computationally expensive and demanding in terms of pilot sequence length. To address this, this study introduces a novel deep learning framework for 6G JADCE consisting of four components: dimension reduction, a core deep learning network, an active device detector, and an estimator for the channel state. A feature learning pre-processing stage followed by an adaptive-tuning mechanism is incorporated, utilizing an internal network comprising Expectation-maximization (EM) and back-propagation to collaboratively refine precision and determine distribution parameters for the device state matrix. Furthermore, an efficient feature-aided adaptive-tuning neural network architecture was established through a combined inner and outer layer-by-layer training approach. Through both theoretical derivation and simulations are validated, demonstrating the proposed framework's superior low complexity and reduced pilot requirements in real-world applications.

Precise, time-stamped detection is fundamental for photonic quantum technology. This precision becomes markedly difficult within distributed networks featuring independent and drifting clocks for spatially distinct nodes. Drawing from recent progress utilizing single photons for time-transfer protocols, we introduce and evaluate a rapid postprocessing algorithm compatible with pulsed single-photon sources, achieving an average root-mean-square synchronization jitter of 3.0 ps. This method delivers stability rivaling systems equipped with ultra-stable clocks (50 ps stability at a 50-second integration period in terms of Allan deviation). This technique offers broad compensation of timing errors from oscillators, outperforms standard algorithms in weak optical conditions, and facilitates concurrent operation of temporal data metrology with the transmission of logical information along existing networks.

Exploration into how opinion dynamics simulations reflect the relationship between influence, homophily, and resulting echo chambers holds significant importance in the social sciences. Our findings demonstrate that this mechanism naturally fosters "echo chambers," creating isolated clusters of like-minded agents. Whereas most analytical techniques demand bespoke derivations for distinct kernel types, our framework utilizes automated symbolic algebra and differentiation, capitalizing on inherent analytical kernel characteristics without manual derivation. Existing methods typically flatten code and queries as token sequences, often overlooking structural details. Furthermore, though Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven capable of modeling program semantics, they struggle to capture long-range global dependencies, which constrains their overall capacity. To tackle these issues, this study presents GraphSearchNet, a framework designed to perform accurate searches by simultaneously modeling rich representations of both programs and natural language queries. Specifically, the approach builds directional graphs employing Bi-directional Graph-based Convolutional Networks (BidGGNN) for the code and queries to capture immediate local structures. Additionally, the framework integrates a multi-head attention mechanism with BiGNN to capture long-range global connections that graphs alone miss thereby enhancing model effectiveness. Comprehensive experiments using the CodeSearchNet benchmark for Java and Python code demonstrate that GraphSearchNet significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

**Background:** The kidney exchange problem (KEP) focuses on pairing patients requiring器官replacementwith compatible live organ donors. Ideally, broader participation across many medical institutions increases the probability of successful matches. However, adherence to current legal standards relies on complex policy-driven privacy measures, which inadvertently prevents smaller facilities from joining the network. Using secure multiparty computation (MPC) offers a viable approach: satisfying regulations for highly sensitive health data through technical methods while alleviating bureaucratic burdens.

**Results:** This research introduces, builds, and evaluates SPIKE, an MPC-based, privacy-first protocol that solves the KEP by identifying matching donor-recruit networks. SPIKE can match 40 donor-patient pairs within 2-person cycles in under 4 minutes, achieving a 400x speedup over existing state-of-the-art systems while delivering medically stronger solutions.

**Conclusions:** The findings demonstrate how to resolve the KEP effectively while maintaining robust privacy guarantees and practical efficiency. Applying MPC techniques fulfils necessary privacy regulations via technical implementation, enabling smaller healthcare providers to directly engage in kidney exchange with fewer legal hurdles.

The geometry of rough, fractured, and porous media is characterized by topological complexity and is frequently approximated using capillary tube bundles in models. However, angle-based geometries provide a more realistic depiction of these internal structures. A defining geometric feature common to these systems is the open, wedge-like channel. According to the classical formulation of capillarity—which neglects intermolecular interactions and assumes the liquid enters from a concave gas-liquid interface—fluid propagation into the wedge will theoretically continue along its spine indefinitely; a phenomenon termed as a concave boundary condition. However, this current analysis demonstrates that steady-state liquid rivulets violating the classical boundary condition can indeed emerge within such channels when surface forces are incorporated into the model. Using an outline developed via disjoining pressure theory, the study examines the morphological configuration of rivulets formed in the wedges, while also accounting for the specific condition in which the wedge walls exhibit flexibility to deformation induced by the liquid.

In distinction from the spin-1/2 fermions, spin-3/2 particles exert minimal effects on the muon's anomalous magnetic moment.

Many organizations rely on online review systems to cultivate their brands and disseminate their messages.
