Deep reinforcement learning has proven effective across various difficult domains. However, traditional Online RL job schedulers, despite their ability to learn optimal scheduling strategies, can be extremely slow, requiring thousands of timesteps for exploration and adaptation from their initial random neural networks. Furthermore, many RL schedulers neglect the value of leveraging historical information and building on established heuristic baselines. Offline RL offers the distinct advantage of policy optimization based entirely on pre-existing datasets, eliminating the need for interaction with the live environment. Aligning with the growing trend toward data-driven approaches, this work examines Behaviour Cloning and Offline RL methods designed to derive policies from logged actions without environmental interference. These methodologies mitigate practical concerns regarding high data collection costs and operational safety for applied Real-World scenarios. While experiments confirm that data-driven approaches yield satisfactory outcomes, they also reveal that performance remains heavily constrained by the quality of the available history. Finally, the introduction of effective prior expert demonstrations for pre-training bypasses inefficient random exploration, enabling rapid alignment with a functional policy during fine-tuned online training. Specifically, the proposed framework employs a foundation of Offline RL sourced from historical actions generated by ideal or heuristic planners, allowing for robust initial training while remaining adaptable to continuous improvement via future online interactions.

To address escalating global economic instability and evolving international relations, nations require resilient, autonomous regional trade systems capable of effectively fulfilling domestic needs. While crucial for food sustainability, the latent potentials of India's inland trade have not been fully realized. We present a comprehensive investigation contrasting agricultural supply chains with flows of other commodities across India, analyzing their spatiotemporal development from 2010 to 2018. Comparing network characteristics and total trade values for both systems, we observed a growth in annual volume of nearly 37% for non-agriculture and approximately 87% for agricultural commodities over the eight-year span. However, a mere increase in total trade value accompanied by minimal improvement in network connectivity suggests an unsustainable over-reliance on specific export hubs within India. Furthermore, agricultural networks demonstrate a more balanced distribution between importing and exporting connections; conversely, states that are significant in agricultural exports also maintain high agricultural import levels. Ultimately, this research establishes a data-backed framework of India's inland trade dynamics, enabling better design strategies for robust and resilient domestic networks.

Single index models offer efficient dimension reduction in regression tasks, particularly for high-dimensional datasets, by transforming complex multivariate predictors along a specific directional vector. We present a new single index framework designed for regression scenarios where the response variable is a random object belonging to an abstract metric space and the predictors are multivariate vectors within a Euclidean space. This model accommodates intricate, non-Euclidean data forms such as univariate probability distributions, covariance matrices, and network Laplacian graphs, all situated within metric spaces. Although Fréchet regression allows us to establish the conditional mean of these random objects based on Euclidean vectors, it lacks traditional parametric regression components like slopes and intercepts because metric-space values cannot be manipulated linearly. In our study, we demonstrate that for Euclidean multivariate predictors, a single index together with its associated projection vector can replace the otherwise missing parametric structure typically reserved for Fréchet regression. Specifically, we establish the asymptotic consistency of appropriate estimators for these indices, contingent upon an identifiability constraint. Furthermore, we derive estimates for the link function of the proposed single index Fréchet regression model using the technique of local Fréchet regression. We evaluate the model's finite sample performance via simulations, addressing both distribution functions and graph adjacency matrices. Additionally, we apply the methodology to resting-state fMRI datasets derived from the ADNI research project.

Traditional adversarial attacks against deep neural networks typically depend on a constrained optimization strategy to create a solitary perturbation for a specific input; however, this study reframes the challenge as devising a distribution of adversarial perturbations, allowing for the generation of varied attack distributions from any unpertected input. We demonstrate that this approach serves as a domain-agnostic framework, capable of targeting various input types with negligible alterations. Evaluating across distinct domains—including visual, textual, and structural data—our method achieves whitebox attack success rates comparable to, and in some cases surpass, current best practices, specifically setting a novel state-of-the-art for graphs. Furthermore, we illustrate that this system efficiently produces a diverse array of attacks for any single input and possesses the ability to zero-shot attack unseen test examples, highlighting significant attack generalization.

These findings provide practical mechanisms to counteract avalanches; the proposed framework can further extend to other complex processes where large-scale simulations demand substantial resources.

Model predictive control (MPC) serves as an optimal strategy that forecasts future system states and determines ideal control inputs to achieve desired reference values. MPC computations occur at fixed sample intervals across a defined finite time horizon. The selection of these intervals and the horizon duration directly balances performance against computational load; a longer horizon with frequent sampling enhances input estimation for rapidly changing states but incurs high costs. Conversely, for states that change slowly, this extensive horizon is redundant. In such cases, reducing the horizon and sampling frequency maintains performance while significantly cutting computational expenses. This paper introduces an adaptive MPC grounded in regression, which derives the most suitable horizon length and sampling count by analyzing dynamic state features via a pre-built synthetic training dataset. A support vector regression model trained on this data executes the predictions. Comparative experiments on linear and non-linear model systems indicate that this proposed method achieves a superior reduction in computation time, lowering costs by 35% to 65% against state-of-the-art alternatives, with minimal sacrifice in overall control accuracy.

Advancements in Virtual Reality (VR) technology, alongside growing access to VR-capable devices, have paved the way for numerous consumer-facing applications. Word embeddings function as fixed symbols representing a word's context based on its co-appearances within a large text dataset. Leveraging this concept, we developed a method termed "interactive refitting." This system adapts embedding post-processing to resolve significant qualitative deficiencies in standard word embeddings. Crucially, the approach empowers users to interactively diagnose and mitigate quality issues rather than delegating decisions about what defines bias to an automated authority. It allows specific entities and departments of an organization to address unique concerns in an iterative manner at a detailed level, while also yielding deeper insights into how modifications to these embeddings propagate through the broader machine learning process.

This paper investigates how quantum resources can achieve more accurate measurements, focusing specifically on whether the hallmark divergence associated with quantum phase transitions (QPTs) remains feasible for precision under environmental noise. While quantum-criticality protocols were previously recognized as efficient and operational in decoherence-less settings, our analysis uses the quantum Rabi model (QRM) to derive an analytical form of the normalized inverse variance. Our results indicate that noise typically causes this variance to converge over time. However, as the system nears the critical point in noisy conditions, the peak inverse variance still follows a power-law growth pattern. Crucially, though, the exponent (approximately -1.2) yields a significantly lower maximum absolute value compared to ideal, noise-free scenarios (which is 2). Furthermore, this variance scales according to power-law relationships with both relaxation rates and temperature. Due to noise's detrimental impact, suggesting improved metrological performance, we propose applying an initial squeezing state to counteract these effects. Expanding this study to two-photon relaxation processes yields a starkly different picture: unlike single-photon cases, the dynamics do not display consistent frequency oscillations. Most notably, while the maximum normalized inverse variance still follows a power-law relative to the energy gap, the exponent reverses to positive and is contingent on dimensionless coupling. Consequently, contrary to noise-free assumptions, two-photon non-linear effects can degrade rather than boost measurement precision via the increased normalization of variance.

This present work narrows that gap by combining audioLIME, a source-separation-driven explanation technique, with perceptual features at a higher processing level. This fusion creates an intuitive chain from raw audio input to emotion output, a method validated by successfully identifying biases in an emotionally skewed prediction model.

We propose a novel approach that manages both static and dynamical electron correlations effectively by applying perturbation theory to a spin-extended Hartree-Fock (EHF) reference state. Our findings show substantial improvements in molecular excited vs. ground states and potential energy curve accuracies when calculating singlet-triplet splitting, significantly surpassing results obtained solely from EHF and standard MP2 methods.

We instead propose a correction rooted in surface tension thermodynamics: for properly corrected Savart-Taylor sheets, the well-known constant and velocity uniform characteristic—adhering strictly to $1/r$ thickness variation dictated by Bernoulli's principle—is restored. Regarding circular hydraulic jumps ourselves, we introduce a straightforward approach based on a combination of Watson's central flow description (\cite{watson_JFM}) and suitable boundary conditions applied to the circular frontal interface. Depending on the particular scenario, this recovers both the scaling originally identified by Bhagat (2018) as well as the longer-recognised conventional scaling dating back to Bohr (1993). We aim in describing under what precise circumstances each regime is required to reconcile new observations from Bhagat with existing hydraulic jump modeling. Yet, the unresolved matter of whether a critical Froude number imposed at the jump's exit and generating logarithmic scaling corrections remains an open problem waiting solution.

An extensive body of work from academics and industry experts has already examined potential coexistence aspects; however, practical research and real-world data regarding how these networks interact are sparse. These experiments indicate that LAA remains difficult for Wi-Fi when both networks simultaneously aggregate channels within dense, urban settings, signaling the need for additional follow-up work.

This study examines the relationship between a convergent sequence of lattices and the corresponding sequence of their set-theoretic Voronoi cell approximations. A hallmark of numerous marine dinoflagellates is their bioluminescence, often seen igniting nightly waves or seawater disturbed by a ship's bow. Although the intracellular biochemistry generating light in these organisms is well known, how mechanical forces induce this glow remains obscure. Results indicate a viscoelastic behavior where luminescence intensity relies on both the magnitude and velocity of deformation, a pattern consistent with stretch-sensitive ion channels operating. Consequently, a mathematical framework successfully mimics these experimental findings.

The Extended Generalized Pareto Distribution (EGPD), developed by Naveau et al. in 2016, constitutes a distribution family designed to model the entire spectrum of a positive random variable, while applying peak-over-threshold methodology to both its lower and upper tails. This article seeks to extend the utility of the EGPD by enabling analysts to integrate covariates into the framework. Specifically, we define a model wherein the parameters function as a additive dependency space or time covariates. Alongside this, we offer a flexible R code add-on that provides generic support for implementing the EGPD, facilitating the integration of various other parametric structures. We apply the capabilities of our R tool to hourly rainfall data in North-western France and offer a discussion on modeling strategies using the example.

Utilizing the characteristics of the MAL distribution, we also present a novel portfolio optimization technique designed to minimize overall risk while regulating standard features observed in financial markets. Through evaluations on both synthetic and actual datasets—specifically using weekly returns for three leading stock indices—we demonstrate that this method surpasses existing models and delivers superior risk measurement accuracy compared to univariate alternatives, avoiding unnecessary repetition.

Recent efforts leveraging Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for Traveling Salesman Problems (TSP) indicate that while DRL-based algorithms are swift and competitive with traditional heuristics on small datasets, they struggle with generalization as instances grow larger. The architecture synthesizes a multilayer perceptron, a graph neural network, and an attention mechanism to establish a stochastic policy that incrementally constructs a TSP solution. Empirical evidence confirms that MAGIC outperforms other DRL methods on random TSP instances regarding solution quality and scalability. Furthermore, the method matches or exceeds standard heuristics and other leading solutions in both computational efficiency and overall performance.

Reconstruction of three-dimensional scenes in endoscopy remains an arduous task due to challenges involving deformities, perspective-dependent illumination, and the repetitive, self-occuding nature of tubular organs like the colon. We introduce SimCol, a new methodology that explicitly models a bimodal probability distribution for endoscope pose prediction, along with corresponding synthesized data. SimCol replicates real-world motion patterns to expose the insufficiencies of current techniques. We offer 18,000 labeled RGB images featuring simulated depth and poses and an open-access Unity-based data synthesis environment after rigorous comparison of various pose prediction frameworks. Results show not that these models generalize from simulation to reality, but that this specific bimodal procedure surpasses existing uni-modal approaches.

Ranking, recommendation, and retrieval systems form the backbone of online ecosystems across various sectors such as commerce, media, admissions, freelance work, and employment. Lately, a substantial body of research dedicated to "fair ranking" has emerged, aimed at ensuring these mechanisms are equitable for individuals, providers, or content alike. Yet, the prevailing literature tends to evaluate fairness within isolated ranking instances, using mere additive metrics across sequences of retrieval events. This analysis critically reviews this field by highlighting how this narrow approach overlooks crucial, situation-dependent issues: the disparity between top search placements and the genuine value received by those ranked, dynamic compounding influences over time, emergent game-theoretic behaviors, and the impact of statistical variance. We subsequently outline a comprehensive, real- Impact-focused future trajectory for fair ranking research, incorporating methodological insights from adjacent disciplines and the potential for stakeholders to dissolve data scarcity and craft robust regulatory frameworks.

This study investigates the zero-temperature-frequency charge current noise in metal-molecule-metal junctions existing within thermal media, where sequential charge transport follows a classical master equation. We analyze the dependence of charge transmission on key parameters: reorganization energy of the surroundings and relaxation dynamics. Interestingly, the classical expression for current noise mirrors the quantum counterpart in structure, both reflecting charge correlations arising from the bridging molecule. Furthermore, we compute an electrochemical junction within this Marcus regime by establishing the Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation, delineating the limits on correlations between average current, its fluctuations, and rate in entropy production in electro- to chemical junctions. Subsequently, applying this methodology to a representative photovoltaic cell allows the calculation of the limit conditions and predicts its ceiling efficiency for transforming environmental power into functional work.

Our proposed approaches utilize one and two-stage object detection architectures trained with expertly annotated datasets. This session will evaluate algorithms capable of copyspace detection and illustrate how they function within generative design systems and workflows like Einstein Designer.

Reliably delivering broadband services relies heavily on understanding the delay profiles of systems utilizing random linear network coding. Earlier research primarily examined network coding over large finite fields or utilized Markov chains for delay distributions, yet overlooked how transmission deadlines influence delay metrics. This study investigates generations of source packets as they are encoded and sent across an erasure broadcast channel, with the specific constraint that a generation is discarded and the system moves to the next once a set deadline elapses, even if not fully received. The authors derive closed-form solutions for the mean number of transmissions needed per generation, factoring in parameters such as the packet generation size, field size, packet erasure rate, chosen deadline, as well as a refined upper bound on average decoding delay that surpasses earlier literary limits. Furthermore, the analysis suggests this framework serves to optimize system parameters by confirming packet volumes remain within optimal bounds—avoiding both undersupply on the broadcast network as well as unnecessary excesses.

Answer retrieval aims to select the most aligned solution from numerous options in response to a specific query, relying critically on the learning of vector embeddings. Two vital indicators in acquiring these representations are the semantic relationship and the specific linguistic structures between questions and answers, as well as their alignment degree. Although previous approaches have focused on dual-encoder frameworks or dual variational auto-encoders using generative techniques such as question-document or document-query modeling, the separation between alignment learning and semantic learning has often prevented the effective acquisition of unified Q&A semantics. This work addresses these gaps by employing a novel cross-variational attention auto-encoding mechanism that generates answers using aligned queries and queries based on aligned responses, ensuring tight integration. Experimental validation on the SQuAD dataset confirms that our proposed framework surpasses the performance of current state-of-the-art methods.

Since its inception within the realm of cryptocurrency, Blockchain technology has evolved into a cornerstone of modern industry by offering key attributes that deliver robust, automated, and resilient operations across various core tasks. However, embedding Blockchain technology amidst diverse industrial systems reveals significant design, security, and privacy hurdles; these present severe threats to both users and data integrity. While prior efforts have attempted to tackle the specific security and privacy needs of particular applications by adjusting relevant parameters, comprehensive research is still required regarding the challenges, requirements, functional demands, possible attacks, and countermeasure strategies for Blockchain-enabled solutions in the industry. This paper provides a state-of-the-art review of such systems in the context of Industry 4.0, with an emphasis on essential security and privacy mandates alongside the associated attack vectors and defenses. Additionally, we evaluate and classify diverse security and privacy methods employed in these environments to facilitate the enhancement of protective features. Finally, our analysis identifies critical unresolved issues within industrial applications to guide the creation of secure, future-oriented Blockchain integrations.

This research analyzes the three-body problem within the framework of parameterized post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism, specifically addressing a coplanar setup belonging to fully conservative theories defined by the $\beta$ and $\gamma$ Eddington-Robertson parameters. The study demonstrates that collinear and triangular equilibrium states can emerge; these represent extensions of the general relativistic Post-Neutronian configurations. While the collinear solution permits arbitrary mass ratios, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ values without restriction, the triangular configuration is contingent upon the nonlinearity $\beta$, though unaffected by $\gamma$. An equilateral formation exists only under specific conditions: all three bodies must have equal finite mass, or two be test masses orbiting a massive body. Generally, when masses differ, the Post-Neutronian triangle fails to be equilateral. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that displacements from standard Lagrange points $L_1$, $L_2$, and $L$ are functions of both $\beta$ and $\gamma$, whereas shifts relative to $L_4$ and $L$ depend exclusively on the $\beta$.

A key prospective use of neural-network quantum states is simulating the time evolution of many-body quantum systems, an aim we achieve by applying these states to emulate the implicit midpoint rule. By doing so, we maintain the conservation of the Hamiltonian system's symplectic structure throughout this approximation. We further ensure that our neural networks, composed of complex-valued parameters, operate as holomorphic functions; leveraging this characteristic allows for efficient gradient computation. When tested on both one- and two-dimensional lattices within the transverse-field Ising model, the method delivers accuracy comparable to that of the stochastic configuration method described by [Carleo and Troyer, Science 355,602-6 (2017)] with a crucial distinction: our approach renders unnecessary the calculation of the (pseudo-)matrix inverse.

Compressed sensing represents a powerful technique widely employed for signal reconstruction across many fields, yet its integration with scanning tunneling microscopy has been slow despite the potential benefits of reduced scanning periods and improved noise resilience. This study implements a basic compressed sensing approach, utilizing a weighted iterative thresholding reconstruction algorithm, on high-resolution STM imagery of both superconducting environments and adsorbed molecular species. We also identify specific methodological shortcomings, such as pattern-related artifacts that intensify in images possessing inherent long-range disorder, along with proposed mitigation strategies. Furthermore, the analysis explores the compressibility of raw STM images to quantify intrinsic noise and predict CS reconstruction success before applying the algorithm, offering a computationally cheap means of estimating effectiveness.

In dense astrophysical contexts like the early universe and supernova explosions, collective neutrino oscillations may be crucial for lepton flavor transport. Securing Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) inference within resource-limited embedded devices, such as low-end FPGAs, represents a rapidly expanding field of research. Secure methodologies often enable third-party designers of FPGA hardware remain ignorant of the network's input and output classification layers. This paper establishes that hardware intrinsic attack mechanisms can still bypass these "secure" designs. The proposed method injects attacks directly into mathematical operations at each layer of a single hardware design, propagating erroneous logic through subsequent layers until misclassification occurs. As this attack is completely random and non-periodic, detection becomes significantly more challenging. We designed and assessed five distinct attack scenarios for various layers, analyzing their performance against an unimpacted implementation in terms of overhead resources and reconfiguration frequency. Our evaluation across two specific architectures demonstrates that latency increases are negligible (under 0.61%), while usage of DSP slices, LUTs, and Flip-Flops (FF) grows to no more than an additional 2.36%. Notably, three attack scenarios require zero additional on-chip BRAM resources. In two specific instances, BRAM requirements increase against a corresponding trade-off reduction in FF and LUT counts. To the authors' current knowledge, this study pioneers research into hardware intrinsic CNN attacks executed by adversaries lacking complete intelligence on the network structure.

Federated Learning (FL) is a critical approach to mitigating privacy and data governance concerns in machine learning (ML), while adversarial training has become a primary defense against inference evasion. Recent years have witnessed large-scale numerical simulations playing a pivotal role in estimating blast event impacts within urban settings to enhance metropolitan safety and security. However, the prohibitive computational costs associated with these simulations, often requiring significant time for individual runs, restrict their applicability to parametric studies. Consequently, this study aims to enable real-time, multi-query analytics through the utilization of Reduced Order Models (ROM), bypassing intrusive approaches. We introduce a Deep Learning-based (DL) ROM framework specifically tailored for capturing rapid transient dynamics and solving parametric partial differential equations characterized by nonlinearity and time-dependence. While standard Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), reliant on linear mode superposition, is insufficient for such problems, our proposed piecewise POD-DM approach offers a robust alternative. This local ROM strategy involves partitioning the time domain and performing an initial linear dimensionality reduction with POD, subsequently employing pretrained autoencoders for a second, nonlinear dimensionality reduction step. Deep neural networks in forward mode then reconstruct the solution from the resulting latent space across both time and parameter variables. This study addresses the One-Shot Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (OODA) challenge, distinguishing it from traditional UDA by accommodating a setting with only a single unlabeled target example. The style transfer module iteratively seeks more challenging stylized instances specific to the one-shot target around the solitary sample as training progresses. This drives the task model to learn from difficult, barely observable styles within the new domain, effectively improving performance even with scarce data. The adversarial design creates a reciprocal dynamic between the two modules, allowing the style extraction and task adaptation processes to continuously benefit from their interactions. Prior research has predominantly concentrated on facial expressions to detect emotion, paying less attention to bodily movements. This study centers specifically on analyzing body affect. Since affect rarely appears in isolation, humans typically pair emotional states with physical actions during natural interactions; an instance of this is a person speaking while smiling. Utilizing Conditional Restricted Boltzmann Machines as our foundation, we adapt the architecture with a factored multi-task component to create Multi-Task Conditional Restricted Boltzmann Machines (MTCRBMs). Upon evaluating this approach using the public Tower Game dataset and Body Affect dataset, we demonstrated that our method not only achieves better classficaiton performance than the state-of-the-art but also possesses proven generative capabilities.

Detecting beats in vocal recordings without musical accompaniment holds promise for applications in music production, song arrangement, and social media. However, a core obstacle lies in the absence of distinct rhythmic and harmonic structures typical of general musical analysis, a difficulty that even humans struggle with; consequently, existing beat-tracking algorithms often underperform when applied to isolated vocals. To address this, we introduce singing beat tracking and the first dedicated solution for it. Our methodology capitalizes on the semantics of human speech by integrating front-end representations generated from the pre-trained, self-supervised WavLM and DistilHuBERT models, alongside a self-attention layer to generate beat predictions. To develop the system, we constructed both training and test sets of separated vocals tagged with corresponding beats using a pipeline involving separation algorithms, beat detection on full tracks, and manual annotation refinement on the VocalGTZAN dataset of 741 vocal stems. The proposed system significantly surpaisses several state-of-the-art general beat-tracking techniques on this dataset in terms of overall accuracy. Furthermore, ablation studies validate that utilizing self-supervised speech representations yields superior results compared to relying on generic spectral features.

End-to-End Spoken Language Understanding (E2E SLU) has gained significant attention because it offers joint optimization and low latency, outperforming traditional cascaded pipelines. However, this architecture overlooks the impact of the final NLU probability on transcript generation, fails to immediately correct ASR errors based on the evolving prefix of the transcript during decoding, and lacks streaming capability since NLU must wait for full audio processing before inference, thereby increasing system latency. However, current programming techniques for complex, constraint-heavy maneuvers are generally inefficient, creating an immediate demand for swifter and more intuitive robotic instruction methods. This study presents an integrated framework combining visual servoing based on Learning from Demonstration (LfD) with force-based Learning by Exploration (LbE), designed to simplify contact-intensive task training and significantly reduce required user effort. Two complementary approaches were developed: the visual servoing method maps human motion to robotics, adapting the demonstrated trajectory according to detected contact zones; conversely, the force-based approach leverages reinforcement learning. Experimental validation comparing instruction and execution efficiency for constrained tasks confirmed that the proposed framework outperformed existing methods across all key metrics, including shortened setup time, higher execution success rates, reduced collision risk, and enhanced usability.

Software has evolved into a pivotal asset across many products and organizational workflows, with an organization's agility in seizing market opportunities hinging on its capacity for continuous improvement. Continuous engineering offers significant benefits compared to sprints or plan-driven models; nonetheless, integrating such a pipeline within established firms poses substantial challenges. This invited position paper identifies adoption hurdles and advocates for a rigorous framework to guide the implementation of continuous engineering. Our insights draw upon collaborative work with several industry partners alongside lessons derived from practical realities and cutting-edge research findings in the field.

The paper concludes that successful adoption necessitates a deep analysis of the target organization, its specific goals, and existing constraints. Because no universal approach works perfectly for every purpose—though core principles widely apply—organizations should anticipate varying levels of maturity and realization of benefits. Primary obstacles to achieving a seamless software flow frequently involve suboptimal organizational structures and a misalignment among teams. Eliminating these structural barriers paves the way for employing automation to accelerate the delivery and quality of software products.

Recent experimental work indicates that humans possess the capability to generalize and form predictions for categories despite lacking exposure to any example instances thereof (Malaviya et al., 2022). Motivated by this, Sucholutsky and Schonlau (2020) proposed a machine learning methodology designed to replicate such generalization. Using synetically generated datasets, they demonstrated sub-linear scaling and confirmed that classifiers can identify among N classes using only M training samples, where M < N, effectively enabling a less-than-one-shot learning regime. Nevertheless, their original approach was restricted to univariate data or simple multivariate scenarios (Sucholetky et al., 2021). In this paper, we broaden this method's applicability to large, real-world, high-dimensional datasets through experimental evaluation within this demanding setting. Specifically, we leverage this technique to tackle new NLP tasks using minimal data samples (4, 8, or 16 instances). Our pipeline first constructs compact, sophisticated less-than-one-shot representations known as "soft-label prototypes" on the training data; these capture the distributional dynamics of the various input-domain classes. Subsequently, a modified k-Nearest Neighbors algorithm is employed, proving that these prototypal representations can yield classification performance that remains highly competitive—or even surpass—significant existing complex few-shot learning techniques.

Stylized three-dimensional avatars are becoming increasingly prevalent in daily life. However, manually generating these avatars typically demands extensive time because it requires average users to laboriously select and adjust a complex mix of continuous and discrete parameters. While self-supervised techniques have emerged to automatically produce high-quality 3D avatars from selfies with minimal annotation costs, they currently struggle with stylized avatars due to significant domain gaps in style. This work introduces a novel self-supervised learning framework designed to create high-quality stylized avatars using combined continuous and discrete parameters. Our proposed approach consists of a cascaded domain-bridging pipeline. First, it employs a modified portrait stylization technique to transform input selfies into target renders that match the desired stylistic theme. Subsequently, it determines the most suitable parameters for these avatars by correlating them with the stylized images, achieved through a differentiable imitator trained to emulate a graphics rendering engine. Furthermore, to facilitate effective optimization of discrete parameters, we utilize a relaxation-and-search cascade. The quality of user identity preservation in our method was evaluated via human preference studies, comparing the results against both manual creation and existing automated techniques; our findings yield significantly higher preference scores than prior works and approximate those generated manually, consistent with an ablation study confirming the validity of our design decisions and pipeline choices.

This thesis focuses on 2+1 dimensional chiral topological phases within quantum matter systems, which are defined abstract by their non-zero chiral central charge, $c$. Subsequent attention shifts to the computational intricacies of these chiral phases. Although Monte Carlo methods typically suffer from the severe sign problem hindering classical simulations for many-body quantum systems, certain phases allow sign-problem-free formulations enabling efficiency. Recent discussions have highlighted the possibility of intrinsic sign problems—where no sign-free representation exists—an area now being explored in the context of chiral topological phases in bosonic and fermionic categories necessitating that the topological spin of anyon is $not$ equal to $e^{2\pi i c/24}$. This thesis confirms, for those systems, the inherent existence of intrinsic sign problems of this kind.

This study investigates an emerging procurement auction model built upon social networks. In a market formed by agents—such as individuals with smartphones or computer systems—a single requester announces demand for goods or tasks to suppliers who have entered the network. Entrant suppliers are further motivated to recruit additional suppliers to join the crowd, creating competitive dynamics among all network participants. A primary challenge in this arena of networked auction is designing the mechanism to motivate every participant to not only truthfully utilize their full capabilities but also actively forward the bidding task to their neighbors in the network. While auctions involving social networks have garnered significant interest over the last few years, prior research mainly focuses on standard upward-based forward auction formats. Additionally, no valid existing network auction model effectively covers multiple types of goods or tasks, with specific attention given to simultaneous consideration of both. Given that typical models only analyze classical downward-based procurnement auctions, no previous valid model simultaneously addresses the complexity of both. We present the inaugural exploration into designing a procurement auction model that incorporates homogeneous and heterogeneous tasks within interconnected social networks. Our theoretical proofs and simulation results demonstrated that, not only do our proposed incentive-aligned, individually rational mechanisms uphold incentive compatibility and are individually rational but we provided rigorous proofs to show that they are both. Across the entire network cost and requester satisfaction metrics, both showed signs of decrease. Our proposed mechanisms were verified through rigorous theoretical proofs to be individually rational and incentive-compatible. Additionally. Our simulations show that systemic cost and requester expenditure can both effectively decline while the mechanism maintains incentive compatibility and individual ration for all suppliers in the system

Autonomous systems frequently rely on deep neural networks due to their capacity to identify complex, non-linear patterns and deliver precise forecasts in dynamic settings. Compounding serves as a productive mechanism for forming words in various languages but presents significant challenges for natural language processing tasks. This study explores whether word vector distributions, also known as embeddings, can facilitate a more knowledgeable analysis of compound structures compared to conventional string-matching techniques. We introduce an unsupervised strategy that utilizes patterns within semantic vector spaces—for example, relationships akin to "to library as to book as to shelf as to book"—to generate accurate compound decompositions. The splitting algorithm, developed based on this analysis, proves especially effective in handling ambiguously compounded terms when performing English-German machine translation. Experiments demonstrate that this example-driven semantic approach surpasses the translation quality of standard frequency-based methods, yielding higher-quality output.

Bipartite graphs illustrate the connections between two non-overlapping groups of entities and are frequently depicted with a two-level arrangement. In this representation, each group occupies a parallel horizontal row, containing vertices where vertices from distinct levels interact through edges curving between the rows. A prevalent optimization goal within these visualizations is to minimize edge crossings, an objective that is resource-intensive and can still yield cluttered diagrams impairing legibility. This study examines a recent technique that eliminates crossings by dividing vertices, specifically aiming to calculate the least amount of vertex splitting required to achieve planarity. The research establishes that deciding if a drawing can achieve planarity after splitting no more than $k$ vertices constitutes an algorithm with fixed-parameter tractability with respect to $k$.

Adaptive multigrid approaches remain highly effective in addressing slow-downs associated with solving criticality in the Wilson-Dirac solver for lattice gauge theory, particularly through multigrid algorithms built on Staggered fermion Kähler-Dirac preconditioning, a success now extended notably to the Summit and Selene architectures. This paper evaluates the four-dimensional performance of the previously discussed Staggered multigrid technique (focusing on Brouwer and colleagues' work from PhysRevd2) while demonstrating an offlining effect—transferring selected aspects of a multi-solve series to the multigrid solver—that has substantially boosted the performance of the MILC spectrum workflows on Summit and Selene.

Recovering accurate geometry and material properties of a scene under unconstrained lighting conditions presents significant challenges. To address this, we introduce a streamlined approach for extracting three-dimensional structure and surface reflectivity from multi-view images captured with ordinary handheld cameras. Our technique constructs a virtual, scene-aligned environment within a differentiable rendering engine, iteratively optimizing it through a stochastic minimization process of photometric error functions. Upon determining these optimal scene parameters, the framework generates photorealistic synthetic views across a wide range of distances and angles. Experimental evaluations involving intricate geometries and diverse reflection characteristics demonstrate the approach's capabilities. Both qualitative visual comparisons and quantitative metrics confirm its superiority in novel view synthesis compared to existing methods.

This paper introduces a pioneering framework designed to leverage both deep learning and atlases for estimating biomarkers in diffusion weighted magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI). While deep learning shows promise in these estimations, atlases are distinctive for modeling the spatio-temporal variability inherent in biomarker distribution. The proposed system utilizes nonlinear diffusion tensor registration to construct biomarker atlases that also generate atlas reliability maps. Similarly, we apply non-linear tensor registration to align the atlas with specific subjects and calculate alignment error maps. These three outputs—atlas-derived biomarker images, reliability maps, and error maps, alongside the original dMRI signal—are fed into a deep learning architecture to perform the final estimation. In a validation cohort of 70 newborns using down-sampled dMRI data, the calculated biomarkers included fractional anisotropy (FA) and measures reflecting neurite orientation dispersion. The results demonstrate that this approach substantially surpasses both standard techniques and existing deep learning methods. Moreover, the proposed method exhibits superior robustness to aggressive down-sampling. Collectively, the findings illustrate how synergizing atlas-based registration with deep learning can achieve previously unreachable accuracy levels in dMRI biomarker quantification.

Although existing literature increasingly examines ceasefires, their ability to fundamentally halt subsequent violence remains ambiguous. Radio Access Network (RAN) virtualization is rapidly maturing, poised to redefine the infrastructure of future cellular networks. By implementing **API Remoting**, PV-RAN executes paravirtualized instances of OpenAIA Interface(OAO) for different slices without the need to modify the OAO codebase. The platform harnesses inter-domain communication protocols within the Xenhypervisor to convey real-time in-phase/quadrature (I/Q) data through shared memory, ensuring virtualization overhead remains negligible. Comprehensive performance benchmarks confirm its minimal overhead and high efficiency.

Furthermore, the solution has been formally integrated with the CyNet Wireless Living Lab, supporting smart agriculture and transportation applications.

Active learning efficiently accumulates informative unlabeled instances for labeling, thereby decreasing the reliance on labeled corpora. We introduce an acquisition function grounded in data local sensitivity and hardness awareness to retrieve these samples. Our approach generates perturbed copies via local modifications and selects original data points displaying the most notable discrepancies in predictive probabilities relative to those copies. Additionally, we enhance our acquisition function by incorporating select-worst-case perturbations, yielding consistent outperformance compared to standard active learning methods across diverse classification benchmarks. We also observe steady gains against existing baselines in studying prompt selection within the context of prompt-based few-shot learning. Collectively, these results confirm that employing an acquisition function guided by local sensitivity and hardness is a robust and beneficial strategy for a wide range of Natural Language Processing tasks.

Given that labeled data is costly and scarce, pre-training strategies serve as the industry norm for ABSA tasks. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the electronic characteristics of polycrystalline lead oxide ($\alpha$-PbO), which forms through a network of single-crystalline platelets with native point defects within its lattice. Although the $\alpha$-PbO crystal is composed of coupled layers, their interaction is so weak that efficient interlayer charge transfer is hindered. Consequently, the polycrystalline structure generates such a high density of lattice defects that conductivity related to these vacancies dominates interlayer charge transitions. Our findings reveal that oxygen vacancies form readily due to low defect formation energy; in their neutral state populated by two electrons, they are prone to donating these electrons to lead (Pb) vacancies, thereby ionizing the deficient pairs of vacancies to generate localized band gap states, which critically influence charge transport. While oxygen vacancies act as deep electron traps situated $1.03$ eV above the valence band edge, lead vacancy functions create shallow holes' traps just $0.1$ eV above the valence band. These calculations successfully explain experimentally observed dark current decay in ITO/PbO/Au heterostructures via charge de-trapping mechanisms occurring at oxygen vacancies.

Traditionally, mass flow modeling relies on hydrostatic balance equations. However, given that momentum transfers often operate on similar magnitude scales along slopes and flow depths, gravitational and inertial effects may become comparable, necessitating a non-hydrostatic approach. In this paper, Pudasaini and Mergili (2019) extend current single-phase Boussinesq models by introducing a new non-hydrostatic formulation designed for multi-phase systems comprising solid particles, fine debris, and viscous fluids. This enhanced framework incorporates advanced gravity terms and dispersion coefficients that account for interfacial momentum exchanges between phases. We outline significant advancements in understanding multi-phase gravity waves arising from phase interactions within non-hydrostatic Boussinesq models. A robust, structured theoretical foundation is provided, emphasizing improved treatment of gravity and dispersion. We discuss scenarios where non-hydrostatic and dispersive influences are particularly critical in such flows, using reduced models to underscore the significance of these contributions. Analytical simplified derivations demonstrate how the new dispersion model can be transitioned into a non-dispersive regime while broadly extending the scope of existing models. We propose an innovative, spatially variable dissipative mechanism termed the "prime-force," which offers precise control over flow dynamics and material run-out, making it highly applicable for professionals in civil engineering and technical practice. Consequently, formally integrating the prime-force into momentum equations is essential. A streamlined dispersion equation is also derived to clarify the fundamental role of dispersion; notably, in the absence of dispersion, velocity remains uniform in a reference state where not in reality, where its presence creates wave patterns in velicity fields—a unique finding in degassing mass movements. Finally, the intensity of dispersion is noted to grow exponentially as solid volume fraction declines or as frictional resistance reduces.

Although deep neural networks now exceed human capabilities in numerous tasks, their effectiveness plummets when the input data distribution varies drastically from training data. Recent studies indicate that adjusting model parameters to fit test inputs can alleviate this drop in performance. Consequently, this paper introduces an updated version of the SwAV self-supervised algorithm by incorporating test sample adaptation. Utilizing SwAV prototypes along with a derived loss function calculated during testing, the approach aligns new, unseen test instances with learned classifications. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method on CIFAR10-C.

Microtubule networks (MTs serve as cellular structures whose appearance reflects exposure to chemical agents and can help identify treatment traits. Consequently, classifying MT imagery holds substantial importance for diagnostic purposes. A significant limitation for human specialists distinguishing the extent of chemical exposure remains a challenge. Automation could substantially impact advancements in cell therapies by enhancing this accuracy. This study investigates applying deep learning to MT classification, evaluated against a comprehensive dataset of animal cell images categorized into three exposure levels of a chemical agent. Our findings indicate that trained deep networks achieve performance matching or surpassing that of trained observers in these classification tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that neural networks significantly outperform human experts specifically in discerning varying levels of chemical exposure.

Achievable superconductivity capable of generating substantial energy gaps in semiconductors even within strong magnetic fields is a critical objective for advancing semiconductor-superconductor hybrid materials in future quantum technologies. This study examines devices comprising InAs nanowires connected electrically to Molybdenum-rhenium (MoRe) superconducting alloys, which are thin films with transition temperatures of approximately 10 K and critical fields surpassing 6 T. We measured an induced superconducting energy gap smaller than theoretically predicted based solely on the transition temperature and noted gap softening under finite magnetic fields, characteristics likely attributable to hybrids employing large-gap Type-II superconductors. These findings support the continued development of devices utilizing MoRe alloys.

Acquiring accurate Downlink channel state information (CSl) at the basestation in Time-Varying Massive MIMO networks faces significant challenges due to the excessive overhead incurred by extensive downlink training and uplink feedback. Addressing this issue, our study evaluates a hybrid precoding architecture at the basestation and proposes a task based on antenna-and-time domain channel extrapolation. By integrating a latent ordinary differential equation (ODE) within a variational autoencoder (VAe) framework, we design a specialized neural network to model the transformation from sparse uplink channel estimates to complete downlink channel states required at the basestation. The architecture utilizes Gated Recurrent Units (GRuS) for the encoding stage and a feedforward neural network as the decoders, optimizing performance through end-to-end training. Experimental simulations validate that this methodology effectively derives full downlink channel information from partial uplink data, substantially lowering the resources needed for channel training.

Comparatively analyzing halo quenching versus black hole (BH) quenching within a semianalytical galaxy formation framework yields distinct results: while both models can align galaxy predictions with stellar mass functions upon calibration, the BH quenching scenario provides a superior fit to passive galaxy fractions as a function of stellar mass ($M_*$) as well as galaxy morphologies plotted against star-formation rate versus $M_*$. Conclining on this central outcome, the study identifies two critical conditions for successful modeling: first, minor mergers utilizing supermassive black hole accretion must be included, or else excessive numbers of luminous galaxies at high masses remain unchecked if minor-merger-dominated systems are never quenched; second, BH growth efficiency via mergers must decline at lower masses—a trend mimicting how supernovae impede growth in environments possessing low escape speeds—so that both the $L_{\rm BH}-M_*$ correlation and the distribution of passive populations match observations aligned with a quasar-feedback regime. This supports the hypothesis where black hole expansion reaches a saturation point effective enough to purge cold galactic fuel and elevate the hot circumgalactic halo's thermodynamic energy, rendering thermal cooling durations inordinately long. Additionally, the study reinforces that galactic shut-down mechanisms involve feedback dynamics differing by magnitude from those sustaining existing states of inactivity.

Spatially distributed systems that evolve over time include complex sensor networks within the Internet-of-Things as well as distributed cyber-physical multi-agent systems; these systems produce large volumes of data with both spatial and temporal components, and designers seek within this data to analyze patterns or uncover structural relationships. Although significant focus has been placed on teaching machines discern causal or logical traits in time-based data through logics such as Signal Temporal Logic (STL)—there remains little dedicated to finding these same relations based on the intersection of space and time. We introduce the first ensemble algorithms designed for unsupervised discovery within the realm of spatio-temporal data. Our methodology involves extracting features directly by projecting the raw data onto the parameter space of a novel parametric logic called PSTREL, or spatio-temporal reach and escape logic. We suggest an agglomerative strategy that hierarchically organizes data to produce groups wherein each cluster corresponds to a unique STREL condition. Our work establishes that this framework can yield STREL formulas of tractable complexity via a novel technique using logic decision trees—and that this advances earlier generic unsupervised approaches tailored for Signal Temporal logic. We demonstrate efficacy through case studies ranging across varied fields, specifically in urban mobility, epidemic spread, green environments, and air pollution surveillance.
This paper offers a concise overview the ethical concerns and the significance of ethically designed algorithms for targeted advertising.

This paper introduces a novel technique for creating spatial constraints to enhance motion planning within dynamic settings. Standard approaches for guiding autonomous vehicles and mobile robots typically depend on map-derived global constraints to produce collision-free trajectories. These methods often falter when no predefined map is available, particularly as the primary source of spatial limits may be rendered invalid by dynamic environmental changes such as traffic jams, construction, or obstacles. While existing triangulation-based strategies offer a means to generate these constraints, they struggle in dynamic contexts and can force a motion planner into unrecoverable configurations. To mitigate this, we propose generating a sequential set of channels that adapt to varying triangulation mesh geometries to function as the necessary spatial guides. Applied to vehicles and robotic agents operating in dense, unstructured terrains, our method is assessed against other triangulation-based algorithms using both simulated scenarios and real-world autonomous driving data. The evaluations demonstrate that our approach yields a superior long-term plan characterized by greater stability, a quicker arrival time, an increased success probability, a higher fulfillment rate, and reduced collisions compared to existing solutions.

This study focuses on developing receding horizon control algorithms tailored to discrete-time linear systems characterized by parametric uncertainty. Unlike many existing frameworks that incorporate process or excitation noise, this work explicitly assumes the absence of stochastic forcing, treating only the parametric uncertainty as the source of randomness modeled via known probability density functions (pdfs). By applying generalized polynomial chaos theory, the paper aims to construct a class of stochastic algorithms that map probabilistic scenarios into an equivalent deterministic problem within a high-dimensional space. Validation of these proposed control strategies is demonstrated through simulations using a linear two-state system.

We introduce the concept of Synchronized Planarity, which addresses an input comprising a loop-free multi-graph alongside specific synchronization constraints. These constraints, for instance, map edges between pairs of vertices sharing the same degree via a bijection, asking if the resulting graph possesses a crossing-free planar embedding where synchronized vertices maintain consistent cyclic edge orders. This paper outlines our approach to designing feedback mechanisms for thruster-augmented walking robots. Assuming the supervisory controller is sufficiently calibrated, we focus solely on adjusting joint trajectory setpoints. We introduce a reference-governor-based intermediate filter that ensures adherence to required performance constraints. Since model modifications or impacts disrupt desired periodic orbits, we ensure hybrid invariance through robust predictive schemes applied within a brief window of the gait cycle; we uniquely employ our robot's thrusters to achieve this invariibility. The primary advantage of our method, compared to existing nonlinear control algorithms based on optimization, is that guaranteed satisfaction of single support phase constraints does not depend on costly numeric computations. Moreover, the proposed control framework for thruster-assisting gaits innovatively permits the targeted use of robustness and performance enhancements throughout the gait sequence, a novelty unrecorded in the current literature.

The AWAKE project serves as a proof-of-concept for proton-driven plasma wakefield electron acceleration, with Run 1 successfully propelling electron beams to 2 GeV. Looking ahead, Run 2 aims to leverage these achievements to reach approximately 10 GeV while enhancing beam quality, necessitating upgrades to both existing proton and electron lines and the introduction of a second plasma cell alongside a new 150 MeV electron injector. This upgraded line must deliver micron-scale stable electron bunches into the secondary plasma cell across a 1-meter span between cells. This paper outlines the design methodologies for this 150 MeV injector, employing tools like numerical optimization and genetic algorithms to satisfy rigorous experimental criteria, while also reviewing operational procedures for both electron transfer systems, including alignment, steering, measuring devices enhanced by neural networks, and optimization techniques.

In response to gaps highlighted by this survey, I conducted a literature review on ML and interaction design to propose matching taxonomy. I explored various feedback patterns that experts express and updates derived in domain expertise. In my proposal I outlined how practitioners can convert expert insights into dataset modifications and/or model improvements based on observations levels or some other type depending upon their input. I concluded my presentation with potential questions regarding my suggestions that offer concrete ways practitioners and experts interact with feedback loops and how these work together in a systemat ic manner going forward.

This study systematically explores short-period orbits in the Lorenz system using similarity signature curves, introducing a novel discovery approach. Drawing on equivariant moving frame theory, the authors derive similarity invariants, alongside which emerges the similarity signature curve—a representation demonstrating markedly more regular behavior than the raw system dynamics. Through integration with a method combining sliding window analysis, the work facilitates numeric detection of quasiperiodic trajectories and successfully locates all periodic orbits with periods $p \leqslant 8$, providing calculations of their period lengths and symbolic sequences.

Graphene-Induced Energy Transfer (GIET), a recently developed method in fluorescence spectroscopy, enables sub-nanometer localization accuracy along a microscope's optical axis. By utilizing the mechanism where near-field energy transfers from an excited fluorescence species to a graphene layer, the technique was initially applied to measure inter-leaflet distances of individual lipid bilayers and analyze membrane structuring within live mitochondria. In this research, GIET was employed to assess nanometric shifts in membrane thickness triggered specifically by the addition of cholesterol within supported lipid monolayers, quantified against varied lipids and rising sterol concentrations. Results confirm that GIET possesses exceptional sensitivity for detecting these subtle structural modifications in biological membranes.

Automating the analysis of tissue sections enhances our comprehension of disease biology and potentially identifies prognostic or therapeutic biomarkers. In the context of digital pathology, detecting biologically significant yet scarce cell types is crucial; however, their infrequency often leads to biased, suboptimal models using standard cell detection methods. To address class imbalance and mitigate these issues, we introduced a deep learning framework trained on a scale of cellular abundance. This approach utilizes "cell weight" images to amplify the importance of rarer cells, integrating these weights into the Dice overlap loss function for regularization. Applied to myeloma bone marrow trephine datasets, the trained model achieved a 0.78 cell detection F1-score—representing a 2% gain over baselines and demonstrating superior recognition of rare cells compared to standard approaches. These findings confirm that adjusting deep learning loss functions based on tissue class abundance enhances detection efficacy. Ultimately, our study underscores the necessity of embedding domain-specific knowledge into algorithms handling pathological datasets characterized by class imbalance.

While models of cardiac electrical excitation and repolarization have advanced in detail, their application in routine clinical practice to guide personalized treatment remains uncommon. A significant hurdle is the ability to calibrate these models despite the scarcity and locality of available measurements taken during standard procedures. This study introduces a novel framework designed for the probabilistic calibrations electrophysiolapytropic parameters within the heart's left atrium using localized data regarding cardiac excitability. This approach models parameter fields as Gaussian processes defined on surfaces and connects them to observed data through surrogate functions that translate local parameter settings into measurable outcomes to derive the resulting posterior distribution of the fields. We demonstrate that this technique can successfully reconstruct specific parameter fields that generated synthetic localized data for effective refractory periods. This method is adaptable to various other clinical measurement protocols and holds broader utility for parameter calibration scenarios involving manifold-dependent variation.

In recent years, attention has shifted toward various manifold reduction techniques. These methods have achieved significant results because it is often valid to assume that complex data resides near low-dimensional nonlinear manifolds; notably, this assumption holds well for functional data. Despite its suitability, the efficacy of these approaches on classical datasets has not yet received systematic testing specifically for functional contexts. Additionally, evaluating the quality of non-invertible embeddings remains problematic due to limited options beyond reconstruction error for performance measurement without invertibility. This paper investigates the specific obstacles posed by the functional data setting for nonlinear dimension reduction. It offers three key contributions. First, it establishes a theoretical framework to systematically examine challenges inherent to functional contexts, adapts existing reduction methods designed for tables or images to this setting, and demonstrates the successful application of these manifold-based tools for curve data. Secondly, the study rigorly and evaluatively assesses a wide range of performance metrics and parameter tuning techniques across diverse functional scenarios, thereby uncovering novel weaknesses that could lead to flawed judgments about embeddings. Finally, the authors propose a detailed methodology that facilitates more reliable decisions regarding the acceptance or rejection of competing representation methods even in their absence of strict conformity.

To address cross-trial variations in effect modifiers with sparse individual patient data, Methods such as Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons (MAIC)—reliant on propensity score weighting—are gaining popularity yet face constraints like limited extrapolation outside observed data and high sensitivity to poor covariate overlap. Conversely, emerging outcome regression models allow extrapolation but typically estimate conditional effects, which are not suitable for the indirect comparisons required. Consequently, recovering a consistent marginal treatment effect demands integrating these conditional results over the population. We introduce a marginalization technique using parametric G-computation that assesses the covariate-adjustment model as a nuisance factor, separating its estimation from the calculation of the target marginal effect. Applicable to generalized linear and Cox models, this framework accepts a Bayesian context to embed the entire analysis within a probabilistic setting. Simulations benchmark the method against both the conventional regression approach and MAIC, demonstrating that our parametric G-computation approach offers superior accuracy and precision, particularly in scenarios with inadequate covariate overlap, delivering unbiased estimates for the marginalized conditional data without failing specific theoretical assumptions to eliminate the bias inherent in the conditional regression approach.

Stabilizing legged robot locomotion on a dynamic rigid surface (DRS)—a surface that moves within the inertial frame—presents a challenging control and planning issue due to nonlinear walking dynamics combined with explicitly time-varying holonomic constraints caused by that movement. This research primarily advances the field by extending the concept of the capture point from static environments to DRS, enabling online motion planning based on this metric. Furthermore, it develops a quadratic-programming-based feedback controller that explicitly accounts for DRS dynamics. Simulation of a quadrupedal robot executing locomotion tasks on a rocking surface validates the stability and robustness of this approach. Compared with a previous method relying on offline planning and input-output linearizing control, which did not ensure feasible ground constraints, these simulations demonstrate notably improved walking performance.

This study outlines findings from targeted searches utilizing {it RXTE} data from various accreting millisecond X-ray pulsars (AMXPs) to identify signatures of non-radial oscillation modes, including r- and g-modes. Our analysis seeks to isolate coherent signals within the neutron star's reference frame by correcting for binary motion-induced phase lags and generating FFT power spectra with continuous light curves comprising up to $2^{30}$ bins, covering frequencies theoretically consistent with both mode types. Examination of the discovery outburst from the 435 Hz pulsar XTE J1751$-$305 yielded one significant candidate: a coherent oscillation occurring at $0.5727597 \times \nu_{spin}$ (249.332609 Hz), exhibiting a fractional Fourier amplitude of $7.46 \times 10^{-4}$. This feature shows statistical significance exceeding the $3\sigma$ threshold at the $1.6 \times 10^{-3}$ level. Potential origins for this mode include rotationally influenced g-modes driven by a helium-rich envelope or a density boundary formed by proton captures within the hydrogen accreted layer. While alternative interpretations such as inertial modes or crustal r-modes remain possibilities, an r-mode explanation would demand an amplitude inducing spin-down effects inconsistent with pulse timing data, thereby excluding this option in favor of the g-mode scenarios. Conversely, no detectable coherent oscillation signals were identified for either AMXP, XTE J1814$-$338 or NGC 6440 X-2. Consequently, we established upper limits for fractional Fourier amplitudes in their respective frequency ranges of $7.8 \times 10^{-4}$ and $5.6 \times 10^{-3}$. Finally, we outline the anticipated viability and sensitivity enhancements achievable in comparable future searches utilizing X-ray missions with expanded collecting areas.

This study explores machine learning (ML) methods that allow intelligent systems to analyze multi-party conversation turn-ordering from dialogue records. specifically focusing on the ability to predict the next speaker based on the identity and content of previous utterances. To evaluate various approaches—ranging from Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) to Support Vector Machines (SVM) and both simple and convolutional neural networks (CNN)—the research analyzes accuracy metrics relative to the use of conversational context data. Experiments were conducted using three corpora: chit-chat data from an American sitcom, logs from a financial multi-bot system, and a topic-focused dataset derived from the Multi-Domain Wizard-of-Oz collection. Key findings indicate that (i) content-based deep learning models benefit greatly from larger corpora; (ii) in small but topic-focused contexts, simple models like MLE or SVE are adequate; (iii) incorporating utterance content with CNN architecture can improve predictions, particularly with limited data.

Hierarchical multi-Dirichlet (MDS and MDPs) priors are increasingly popular, but inferring their mixing weights and parameters is challenging due to the sums-over-tensor terms in these parameters, the complexity of which complicating joint distributions for model post-hindsight. Quantum network nonlocality is realized through non-classical correlations stemming from local measurements across k-party entangled states ($k<N$), which arise within multi-party quantum networks. We present that bipartite entanglement ($k=2$), combined with the post-selection protocol, suffices to generate any quantum network nonlocal effect, unlike scenarios involving strictly non-signaling devices without such adjustments. Conversely, strictly quantum networks utilizing only pure stabilizer states and Clifford gates cannot produce network nonlocality. Thus, these results clarify the distinction among different forms of network nonlocality, demonstrating that all established methods for creating genuine rather than non-genuine correlations necessitate some type of non-Clifford operation.

Mapping Deep Neural Network (DNN) models onto accelerators is a computationally intensive challenge that has spurred significant research into both heuristic and machine-learning approaches to manage complexity. Although numerous existing mappers claim superior performance based on empirical evidence, the field still lacks a systematic understanding of how various search strategies explore the solution space and how different mapping dimensions impact accelerator efficiency. This understanding is vital for designing frameworks capable of handling the intricate mappings of emerging DNN architectures, which are becoming increasingly irregular and sparse, thereby expanding the complexity of their mapping environments. Consequently, this project offers a novel, side-by-side evaluation of search techniques used by current mappers, moving beyond the creation of another alternative. Furthermore, by deriving insights from this comparative study, we introduce two novel augmentation techniques—warm-start optimization and sparsity-aware design—that enhance speed, scalability, and robustness across a wide range of diverse neural models.

Deep learning has popularized deep neural network models for single-input music source separation, with recent research increasingly favoring end-to-end methods operating directly on audio waveforms. Specifically, transforming a mixed input signal into a latent space and applying a soft multiplicative mask often yields the highest accuracy but can generate distorted artifacts within source estimates. To mitigate these artifacts, this paper introduces HTMD-Net, a hybrid time-domain architecture that integrates a streamlined masking unit with a skip connection-enabled denoising module, which refines outputs generated by standard masking procedures. Evaluations conducted on the musdb18 dataset using the single-input singing voice separation task demonstrate that HTMD-Net achieves results competitive with pure masking approaches when trains under Equivalent conditions, with notable improvements specifically for silent segments and greater computational efficiency."

Anatomical entities, including the liver, hippocampus, and bony structures, are often modeled as orientable, closed surfaces. This framework allows for precise calculation of metrics like volume, surface area, curvatures, and Euler characteristics, enabling comparisons across various topologies. While such shapes are typically represented as zero-level sets in curve evolution analyses, practical implementations rely on embedded binary images. Application validation used femur and L4 vertebra data from 50 patients scanned via computed tomography. Results indicate substantial reduction of local curvature distortion caused by the quantization inherent in signed distance maps. A global assessment using regression and Bland‑Altman plots demonstrated superior fidelity for average medial mean cur (coefficient of determination increased to 100%), surface area (proportional bias reduced from –5.0% to +0.6%), and Euler characteristics (accuracy improved to 98%). Overall, the Gaussian-blurring embedding routine provides a reliable method for evaluating curvature on closed, implicit surfaces.

Despite the proven efficacy of diverse Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) variants in estimating cardiac indices, their susceptibility to minor input disturbances—such as spatial transformations, image distortions, and adversarial attacks—remains a concern. Deep learning (DL) has proven highly effective in computer vision (CV), with related methodologies adopted in sectors ranging from security and healthcare to remote sensing. Leveraging DL for CV analysis can therefore uncover crucial details about objects, including their count, positioning, distribution, and movement. This article primarily aims to explore the application of DL-based CV within wireless communications to introduce new dimensions for both theoretical research and practical engineering systems. To demonstrate this application, we illustrate an instance involving a millimeter-wave (mmWave) system optimized for beamforming in mobile settings using DL-enhanced CV. This framework employs ResNet, two-dimensional to 3D ResNeXts, and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to forecast future beam indices based on historical observations and street view imagery from an mmWave setup for Multiple-Input-Multiple-Output (MIMO). Experimental outcomes demonstrate that these frameworks substantially outperform baseline methods in accuracy, indicating that visual inputs significantly boost the efficacy of the MIMO beamforming system. Lastly, we discuss the potential opportunities and existing challenges surrounding the integration of DL-based CV into wireless communication protocols.

This study examines the Conditional Color-Magnitude Distribution (CCMD), defined as the color-magnitude relationship for central galaxies at a specific fixed halo mass, utilizing semi-analytic galaxy formation models (SAM) alongside hydrodynamic simulations. Applying a Gaussian mixture model to halos of varying masses, we determine that the CCMD decomposes almost exclusively into red and blue populations. These populations are nearly orthogonal: the blue component appears as a broad range in color with a tight magnitude constraint, whereas the red component exhibits the opposite characteristic with a broad magnitude span but a narrow color range. Focusing on SAM outputs to trace the origin of these bins, we analyze connections between central galaxy color and specific host halos and galactic traits. For lower-mass halos, central color correlates strongly with assembly history properties; conversely, this correlation disappears in high-mass systems. Various galaxy metrics—including supermassive black hole mass, cold gas reservoirs, and specific angular momentum—influencing central galaxy color are identified. A complementary machine learning approach predicting central galaxy color based on input parameters from the halo environment further reinforces these findings. Notably, color prediction accuracy improves substantially when both halo and galaxy properties are utilized compared to using halos alone. Even with these inputs, subtle gaps persist between predicted and actual CMFs for low-mass systems, while high-mass systems show no uniquely defining traits, pointing toward stochastic processes playing a significant role.
