Experimental results indicate that our proposed approach achieves superior performance and more stable convergence compared to related methods dealing with partial labeling, particularly in scenarios with significant heterogeneity.

The absorptivity of materials constitutes a significant source of uncertainty in numerical simulations used for laser welding and additive manufacturing, a value typically established via trial-and-error calibration. Driven by the growing need for interpretable machine learning, there is a heightened demand for human-generated diverse explanations to clarify model decision factors. To enhance the transparency and trustworthiness of AI systems, the domain of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has developed, splitting into feature attribution and counterfactual explanation approaches. This study seeks to foster trust in time series models by utilizing motifs to create counterfactuals. We evaluated MG-CF on five real-world datasets from the UCR repository, demonstrating its superiority over competing state-of-the-art baselines in balancing the desired properties of counterfactual explanations.

Randomized controlled trials primarily rely on Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) to analyze outcomes. Despite NHST offering long-run error rate assurances, it has a significant drawback: its central tool, the p-value, serves as just an indirect indicator of evidence against the null hypothesis. This limitation exists because the p-value is calculated under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true, thereby disregarding the data's probability under any alternative hypothesis. Consequently, to properly quantify the data's support for or against the null, an alternative hypothesis must be explicitly defined (Goodman & Royall, 1988). Paradoxes emerge when p-values are misinterpreted as direct evidence; for example, data points can be equally surprising under both a null and a plausible alternative hypothesis. In such a scenario, a p-value of 0.045 (statistically significant) might not necessarily reduce the prior credibility of the null hypothesis. This leads to critiques arguing that traditional inference can exaggerate the weight of evidence against the null. Conversely, non-significant results (where p > 005) can still offer meaningful support for the alternative hypothesis. Therefore, it is vital researchers understand when traditional null significance diverges from actual evidentiary strength, which demands calculating and presenting a direct measure of evidence in tandem with the conventional p-value.

Furthermore, our analysis identified two distinct phases: for cities with populations under one million, their centrality is determined primarily by a balance between their degree of connectivity and size; conversely, cities exceeding one million inhabitants tend toward higher centrality, which relies mainly on size rather than connectivity metrics.

Selecting suitable positive examples plays a critical role when object detection methods are trained using convolutional neural networks. This thesis aims to construct a theoretical framework dedicated to studying parameter estimation for quantum channels. Specifically, it analyzes the sequential strategy for estimating unknown parameters encoded via a multiple-uses channel, representing the most comprehensive approach. A central objective is to determine fundamental limits, known as Cramer-Rao lower bounds, for the resulting estimation error; proposed bounds here apply universally across all valid quantum dynamics and can be framed as optimization problems. Furthermore, the work explores "amortization," the use of quantum catalyst states to augment the capability of an estimation strategy. In quantum metrology, a channel's potential depends on its Fisher information, so this thesis introduces a metric called amortized Fisher information to quantify how catalyst enhancement modifies this value for parameter estimation. We demonstrate an "amortization collapse"—proving that specific Fisher information measures remain unaffected by catalysts relative to their utility in sequential versus parallel protocols—to derive bounds derived from the Fisher-information perspective. Within the single-parameter regime, we utilize both the right logarithmic derivative (RLD) and the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) formulations. Moving to multiparameter estimation, where the bounds constitute matrix inequalities, we derive an equivalent RLD-based scalar Cramer-Rao limitation. Finally, for all considered estimation scenarios and parameter regimes, we employ these RLD-derived limits to establish a necessary condition preventing the achievement of the celebrated Heisenberg scaling.

The rapid advancement of automatic anatomical landmark localization through deep learning in recent years highlights a crucial need: quantifying prediction reliability. To enable adoption in critical medical environments, these models must be equipped with mechanisms to detect and rectify errors. We introduce Quantile Binning, a data-driven approach that classifies predictions according to their estimated error ranges based on uncertainty levels. Our framework works with any continuous measure of uncertainty and enables the rapid identification of the most accurate predictions along with their corresponding error estimates. By defining evaluation metrics based on this binning process, it becomes easy to benchmark various uncertainty measures. We evaluate this approach across different epistemic models—integrating aspects of two baselines within U-Net and patch-based localization architectures—using results from three datasets. Our analysis demonstrates that excluding gross mismatches captured within specific Quantile Bins significantly increases the percentage of predictions meeting strict error tolerances. Furthermore, our findings suggest the utility of Quantile Binning even when dealing with aleatoric uncertainty stemming from natural landmark variability, while providing practical guidance on selecting and applying appropriate methods for different scenario. Standard condensed matter theory at room temperature often models electrons in conductors as spatially localized wave packets, diverging from Schr¨odinger equation predictions because the actual mechanism of how finite temperature localizes wave functions remains debated. In this study, we model the environment using a fluctuating potential and examine various unravellings of the Lindblad equation for the one-dimensional tight-binding system. Although every unravelling results in a rapid decay of phase coherence, not all produce narrow wave packets; specifically, quantum-state diffusion unravelling leads to such confinement. Counterintuitively, in this model with stronger quantum-state diffusion, the wave packet width diminishes with noise strength more slowly than the phase coherence length does alongside it. We provide both analytical and numerical evidence for our findings and offer phenomenological explanations. In conclusion, unless interactions between the wave function and environment are included via feedback terms, open quantum systems resist description solely by a single set of unique vectors, representing significant impediments to fully understanding the quantum-classical transition. No other extraneous text has been considered included.

Quantum gravitational interactions in the immediate vicinity of a horizon could drastically transform a black hole's event horizon into a partially reflective structure known as the quantum membrane. Treating such an object as an Exotic Compact Object (ECO) allows us to explore strong gravitational regimes where quantum effects might induce a non-conserved matter tensor within Rastall gravity. By leveraging the Kerr/CFT correspondence, we analyze Kerr-Newman-NUT-Kiselev black holes to uncover their hidden conformal symmetry in the context of Rastall gravity. The 2D Conformal Field Theory provides the microscopic Cardy formula entropy, as well as absorption cross-sections that align precisely with gravitational calculations. Extending this dual CFT analysis to ECOs accounts for gravitational echoes generated by the quantum membrane, appearing as oscillations in the absorption profile: a feature also reflected through Quasi-Normal Modes (QNMs). Comparative studies of ECOs and black halls show the pivotal influence of Rastall coupling constant, particularly as echo time delays explicitly depend on Rastall parameters. Consequently, time-variable measurements could detect these non-linear corrections unique to Rastall gravity, offering potential experimental signatures for its validation.

The digitization of historical maps facilitates the analysis of rare, fragile, and previously difficult-to-access sources, featuring the tracking of primary map characteristics over time for thematic studies. Specifically, we focus on detecting closed structures—such as buildings, building blocks, rivers, and gardens—to observe how their boundaries change over time. Recognize the difficulties that historical maps pose for traditional pattern recognition, the use of Mathematical Morphology alone is often inadequate for detecting closed features, particularly because of cluttered layouts and overlays. Furthermore, leading-era Convectional CNN architectures struggle with this domain: while adept at filtering general content, L cannot ensure the identification of closed boundaries, and the distinctive textural/spectral properties and lack of color data often prevent robust boundary-based detection purely on visual edges. By refining a hybrid framework that leverages the superior edge detection and filtering capabilities of CNN alongside the strict closed-contour guarantee of Mathematical Morphology, we address our contribution in achieving comprehensive shape vectorization. Testing this unified pipeline shows us effectiveness.

Achieving intended controller performance necessitates proper tuning, and the recent DiffTune framework addresses this via computational graph unfolding of dynamical systems and controllers to generate parameter gradients through auto-differentiation. Although effective, DiffTune's standard gradient descent approach ties system performance to the learning rate, and its success is therefore sensitive to the selection of this specific hyperparameter. This paper instead introduces hyperparameter-free mechanisms for controller parameter adjustment. To identify the optimal updates, the method maximizes the reduction in a loss function, specifically targeting a loss estimate derived from predicted system and action states. Two newly proposed update methods were implemented by leveraging loss reduction optimization and subsequently benchmarked against similar variants via simulations of a Dubin's car and an autotrot. Empirical results confirm that the developed first-order approach surpasses hyperparameter-reliant techniques in performance and demonstrates superior stability compared with hyperparameter-free second-order methods.

This review examines the theoretical underpinnings and experimental signatures of wave dark matter (WDM)—a bosonic candidate with a mass less than roughly $30 \mathrm{~eV}$. In galaxies such as the Milky Way, these ultra-light particles possess an average inter-particle distance smaller than their de Broglie wavelengths, permitting an effective classical wave description. Their motivation in particle physics spans various models, including standard QCD axions, axion-like-particles (ALPs), and the "fuzzy dark matter" framework ($m \approx 10^{-22}$ eV). The wave-like properties generate distinct phenomena: first, wave interference creates significant (~unity) density variations on the de Broglie scale. These variations can trap density-depleted regions, known as vortices, where velocity circulates; typically, one such structure forms per de Broglie-sized volume, though the associated halo/subhalo abundance is predicted numerically and remains uncertain regarding suppression at very low masses. Second, particle condensation produces core solitons in haloes; since they oscillate and random scatter over time, these exhibit characteristic interference effects, with numerical simulations required to firming up precise abundance and structural predictions for very low masses. Third, hierarchical substructures from interference in $\sim 10^{-22}$ eV dark matter may be detected through tidal streams and weak/strong lensing, with a distinguishability from sub-halosal basing on the scaling of the lens time-scale versus tidal streams. Furthermore, moderately low masses (axion range) of WDM should present distinct features measurable in stochastic fluctuations of power spectral density within the context of specific lab setups. Current limits and open questions, spanning experiments in modern particle physics labs against astrophysics/cosmos/lens imaging are reviewed.

With ongoing growth in experiment scale and complexity, a primary analytical hurdle involves converting extensive datasets into an accessible and easily interpretable format. Typically, individual data points reflect only pairwise relationships between entities, making it difficult to merge these local interactions into a unified global perspective. This aligns with the classic localization problem, which maps local measurements onto a global framework to uncover a system's inherent structure. In this work, we focus on this task's more difficult variant: bipartite localization, where pairwise distances are restricted to interactions involving two distinct categories—examples include antibody-fungus dynamics, drug-cell effects, or user preferences. We adapt established algorithms to address this bipartite scenario and evaluate their robustness against noise, outliers, and missing observations. To provide a concrete proof of principle for this adaptation to neutralization data involving antibodies versus viruses, an antibody behavior distribution was constructed that captures, among other metrics, that the requirement for strong potency against certain viruses often correlates with reduced potency against others.

Grasping the relationships between structure and properties is vital for effectively designing materials tailored to specific applications. While two-scale simulations are common for assessing how microstructures influence macroscopic component behavior, they often prove computationally intensive, making them unsuitable for multi-query tasks like material design or optimization. To overcome this barrier, microscopic simulations can be substituted with flexible surrogates capable of handling diverse microstructural parameters, though extending existing methodologies to encompass geometrical parameters remains a challenge addressed here. This work builds on prior accurate models using proper orthogonal decomposition and Gaussian process regression by introducing a technique that maps varying geometries onto a parent domain via solutions to an auxiliary linear elasticity problem. By combining these transformations with non-linear microscopic solutions, we develop a rapid surrogate model featuring: effective quantity predictions independent of the auxiliary problem; stress fields adhering to balance laws with periodic boundaries; non-intrusiveness; the recovery of full stress distributions for all geometric configurations; and accessible sensitivities ready for optimization. Validation across composite microstructures accounting for rotation and significant shape variations in inclusions demonstrates high accuracy, while a two-scale optimization case confirms the model's ability to achieve substantial computational speed-ups without sacrificing performance.

The results demonstrate that the problem is **W[1]-hard** under several tight structural constraints: specifically, the feedback vertex set number, pathwidth, treedepth (applied to certain low-pathwidth and low-treedepth deletion settings), and the minimum deletion size required to achieve this pathwidth or treedepth for dense graphs. Furthermore, W[1]-hardness is shown for planar graphs relative to solution size and dense graphs relative to clustering parameters (cluster vertex deletion), including the majority variant of the theorem relative to **treewidth**. While **cliquewidth** on graphs offers polynomial solvability, efficient fixed-parameter algorithms (FPT) are established for parameters measured by **neighbourhood diversity, twin coverage**, and **vertex information**. Additionally, the solution-based **W[1]-hardness parameterization problem for planar graphs** proves that the solution set belongs to FPT when the input graph possesses planar properties. The paper conclusively addresses unresolved challenges posed by **Carlos Bazgan** and **Marcellin Chopin (2014)** regarding the tractability of the **Harmless Set** problem when **solution-based treewidth parameter parameters** are bounded in planar graphs. The problem remains computationally beneficial when measured, but its complexity on dense graphs or large solution spaces is unresolved due to structural constraints.

Sensors and tools are required for extracting critical treatment-aiding data from magnetic resonance (MR) images to automatically segment brain tumors. Artificial intelligence that is aware of its context represents a rising paradigm for deep learning in computer-assisted medical image analysis. Research conducted in this project evaluates if incorporating brain anatomy as white matter, gray matter, CSF probability maps, and binary masks enhances tumor segmentation within U-Net architectures. Utilizing the BraTS2020 dataset, the study formulated two standard 3D U-Net models that utilized these anatomical clues as distinct channels—specifically as Concurrent Image Masks (CIM) or Concurrent Image Probabilities (CIP) alongside traditional MR modalities. A baseline model (BLM) employing only conventional inputs was trained for comparison. The research explored how adding contextual data impacts segmentation accuracy, training duration, domain generalization, and compensation scenarios when fewer MRI modalities exist. The study reveals that there are no statistically significant deviations in Dice scores between baseline models and those incorporating contextual information, holding for both high- and low-grade tumor groups individually. The sole instance where contextual utility is significant is in scenarios requiring segmentation with limited MR modalities. Ultimately, combining anatomical context via binary masks or probability map channels does not yield an overall statistically significant enhancement in segmentation accuracy.

Architectural innovations in deep neural networks have propelled significant advances across numerous computer vision domains. Consequently, Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has developed into an effective strategy for automating architecture design, operating independently of human expert guidance. Although image classification successes reveal promising potential, the capabilities of NAS remain insufficiently validated within more demanding semantic segmentation scenarios. Applying NAS to this field presents two key hurdles: first, the necessity of processing high-resolution imagery, and second, the requirement for real-time inference speeds, which are critical for applications like self-driving vehicles. To address these difficulties, this paper introduces a surrogate-assisted multi-objective framework. By utilizing a sequence of tailored predictive models, this approach recasts the complex NAS challenge into a standard multi-objective optimization task. Further refined by a hierarchical pre-screening mechanism used during infill selection, our method systematically curates architectures that optimize the balance between segmentation precision and processing velocity. Experimental validation across three benchmark datasets, coupled with deployment on a Huwai Atlas 200 DK, confirms that our proposed method consistently identifies architectures that significantly exceed existing state-of-the-art solutions, whether those benchmarks involve human-designed models or outputs from alternative automated NAS methodologies.

Although real music signals exhibit high variability, they inherently possess strong statistical structures. Bayesian modelling allows for the unification of available prior knowledge concerning sound generation physics and the rules governing complex auditory structures, such as individual notes, chords, or entire musical compositions. Traditionally, Automatic Music Transcription algorithms treat specific tasks like multiple fundamental frequency detection and beat tracking as separate operations. Consequently, a significant yet unresolved challenge remains in achieving joint estimation for all these parameters simultaneously. This paper introduces a Bayesian framework for modeling musical audio and conducting content analysis that employs Gaussian processes. This methodology optimizes the simultaneous estimation of various music concepts and integrates into kernel functions a priori insights derived from the signal's non-stationary dynamics and rich spectral variations. We demonstrate the advantages of this approach through evaluations on pitch estimation and the inference of missing data segments within polyphonic recordings.

The field of recognizing online handwriting on standard paper sheets is well-explored, yielding only limited practical success, particularly with earlier sensor-based solutions that hindered real-world usability. In response, we introduce a practical, writer-independent recognition system using a pen integrated with sensors to analyze handwriting on conventional surfaces. Uniquely, no user-specific calibration or prior character training is needed; instead, the user begins writing on standard (possibly unlined) paper. The integrated device features a magnetometer, an accelerometer, and force sensing, effectively digitising the sensor signals. We present the implementation based on a 26 uppercase letter plus 26 lowercase letter per Roman alphabet. The system leverages convolution networks trained on this dataset to automatically classify characters. We present the performances outcomes and discuss the possibility of practical implementation for solving real-time writer- independent handwritten character recognition on standard stationeries for anyone.

Vulnerabilities arise within computer systems due to faults or errors in the architecture, design, or software implementation of these flaws, which malicious actors can exploit to compromise security. The Common Weakness Enumerations (CWE) serve as a hierarchical taxonomy of software defects, offering a framework to recognize weaknesses, assess exploitation impacts, and devise mitigation strategies. Distinct from CWE, Current Versions and Exposures (CVE) provide concise, unique descriptors for identifying specific vulnerabilities found in particular systems. Consequently, classifying vulnerabilities by mapping CVEs to the corresponding CWE classes aids in understanding impact and implementing effective countermeasures. Given that manual mapping is not feasible, there is significant demand for automated solutions.

This paper introduces V2W-BERT, a pioneering Transformer-based framework leveraging techniques from link prediction, transfer learning, and Natural Language Processing. Our method surpasses existing strategies by demonstrating superior performance across the full spectrum of CWE classes—those with ample training data as well as rare instances where historical data is scarce or absent. Furthermore, our approach effectively predicts future CVE-CWE links for future incidents by learning from past data patterns, establishing a robust solution for real-world deployment utilizing resources from MitRE and the National Vulnerable Database. Experimental results indicate achieving up to 97% accuracy using randomly partitioned datasets and 94% accuracy when using temporally ordered splits, highlighting potential to advance cybersecurity methodologies. We anticipate these contributions could shape improved training models and methods for addressing increasingly complex cybersecurity challenges.

Data serves as the primary driver of machine learning advancements in the last ten years, yet acquiring labeled, high-quality data remains difficult and costly. To effectively utilize large amounts of unlabeled data, contrastive self-supervised learning has emerged as a pivotal technique. This approach works by bringing augmented representations of a specific sample closer in the embedding space and pushing representations of distinct samples further apart. This method enables contrastive models to learn highly informative data representations that subsequently improve performance in various machine learning tasks. However, recent findings indicate a susceptibility to privacy attacks. While most prior work focuses on security in supervised learning, similar risks exist within the expressive data samples learned via contrast learning, posing significant privacy vulnerabilities.

This study presents the inaugural analysis of privacy within contrastive learning, specifically examining resistance to membership and attribute inference attacks. Additionally, experiments empirically verify (1) the stated framework equivalence, (2) the explanatory power offered by the Fourier amplitude-phase framework, and (3) the enhanced control affordances achievable at the feature-frequency level.

The adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) in cybersecurity is rising in both academic and industry circles, driven largely by extensive malicious malware attacks targeting critical infrastructure such as cloud networks and state entities. Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS), leveraging various AI methodologies, have become widely adopted for their capacity to process vast datasets with significant predictive precision. These solutions, hosted within the organizational Cyber Security Operation Center (CSoC) as defensive measures, continuously monitor network traffic to safeguard Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA), aiding CSoC analysts in evaluating and addressing potential threats. However, IDS implementations based on Deep Learning (DL) often function as opaque "black boxes," failing to articulate the rationale behind their decisions. Consequently, this lack of transparency hinders CSoC professionals from refining their threat mitigation strategies based solely on model outputs. A proposed remedy involves developing explainable Intrusion Detection Systems (X-IDS). This survey presents current frontiers in Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) applied to IDS, examines prevailing obstacles, and links these challenges to X-IDS architectural considerations. Special attention is given to both white box and black box methodologies, analyzing the performance and explanatory trade-offs inherent to each approach. Additionally, we propose a human-in-the-loop architectural blueprint to guide X-IDS design. We provide specific research recommendations focusing on defining explainability in the context of IDS, tailoring outputs to distinct stakeholders, and establishing standardized metrics for explanation evaluation.

Although dark matter remains a fundamental component of the standard cosmological paradigm—deducted primarily through astronomical observations rather than direct detection of its microscopic properties—its nature is still unclear. This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for understanding Dyakonov-Shur plasma instabilities in graphene transistor systems driven by currents. Through a hydrodynamic approach tailored to any electron drift speed within the two-dimensional electron gas of graphene, we derive governing nonlinear equations for this DS instability. We investigate the conditions required to initiate the unstable state and identify the physical attributes of the subsequent steady-state electron configuration. Our analyses show that such instabilities precipitate coherent anharmonic oscillations of the electron fluid, allowing us to specifically map their spatial profile and quantify the power of electromagnetic radiation emitted by the graphene transistor during the unstable regime.

Conversational Machine Comprehension (CMC) is a specific avenue in conversational artificial intelligence aimed at training systems to grasp open-domain natural language texts and participate in multi-turn dialogues to address queries based on those texts. whereas the majority of machine comprehension research, particularly in Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC), focuses on single-turn question answering, multi-turn CMC has only emerged in popularity due to advances in neural language understanding through architectures like BERT and the availability of large-scale datasets such as CoQA and QuAC. However, this surge in interest has resulted in a proliferation of concurrent publications; each features distinct approaches despite sharing similar underlying structures.

While these works display varying perspectives regarding their position within the existing lit eratur e, the consistent volume of model contributions on relevant datasets has created a pressing need to synthesize fragmented knowledge and facilitate future study. Consequently, this review seeks to outline a comprehensive understanding of CMC with a specific focus on shared tendencies in modern model design, particularly regarding their management of conversational historical context. By constructing a generic framework for CMC and delineating the nuances among recent methodologies, this work is intended to act as a comprehensive resource for the domain for the upcoming research community.

First is tracking emotional status of the user over time; second is a proactive policy that forecasts not just what emotion should be employed to match user sentiment with predictions about user intent. These are then harnessed in directing the generation of fitting responses to that purpose. Results showing dynamic application of this management across emotional and intent nodes allow this proposed solution generate significantly greater sympathy during experiments compared to many leading baseline work under both human judge and system evaluations.

A critical determinant of their robustness is the coupling coefficient between networks, which dictates the degree of load redistribution across them. We derive recursive equations to describe such dynamically evolving systems under changing network coupling. Utilizing these formulas, we develop strategies to bolster the resilience of interdependent networks by adaptively adjusting coupling coefficients in real-time to suppress subsequent failures. Both theoretical derivations and simulations demonstrate that this approach offers a markedly significant improvement over prior methods that rely on static coupling parameters. Furthermore, our proposed Step-wise Optimization (SWO) approach exhibits superior performance in mitigating cascading failures alongside advantages in computational efficiency, scalability to numerous networks, and flexibility against various attack scenarios. Simulatory results confirm the effectiveness of SWO in enhancing robustness against propagation failures across a wide range of network topologies.

Markov decision processes (MDPs) are typically the framework used to define reinforcement learning (RL) problems. However, this research extends beyond MDPs to address RL in environments that are non-Markovian, non-ergodic, and only partially observable. Rather than focusing on practical algorithms, the thesis examines fundamental theoretical questions, such as balancing exploration against exploitation, methods for optimal exploration, and the criteria for agent optimality. We adopt the nonparametric realizable paradigm and first demonstrate negative results regarding Bayesian RL agents, notably AIXI. We prove that arbitrary and adversarial priors can cause these agents to fail spectacularly, revealing that concepts like a prior-free intelligence measure via Legg-Hutter and Pareto balance are entirely contingent on subjective choices about the prior. Further, since every policy is Pareto optimal within the set of all computable environments—all invalidating standard optimality properties for AIXI. Conversely, this study confirms specific approaches in objective Bayesian RL by showing that Thompson sampling is asymptotically optimal within stochastic settings, meaning its expected performance eventually aligns with the best possible strategy. By relating asymptotic optimality to regret under recoverable environments (settings where agents can learn from errors), we show Thompson sampling ensures sublinear regret, leading to better long-term decisions. Collectively, these findings resolve the "grain of truth" issue: Bayesian agents operating with a prior probability that includes the true policies of others will learn these strategies in multi-agent applications. We identify a robust yet countable limit of such truth distributions, enabling smart Thompson sampling systems to converge on and implement Nash strategies in diverse unknown computing scenarios involving strategic interactions among agents.

Securing public safety in a Smart City constitutes a vital yet increasingly intricate challenge, exacerbated by multi-agency collaboration and the expansion spanning cyber and social dimensions. We introduce a finite extensive game with perfect information, designed to simulate strategic interactions and determine optimal resource distribution scenarios during terrorist organization assaults that span both physical and cyber-social infrastructure tiers. Referred to as the Smart City Defense Game (SCDG), the model features three participants starting with fixed budgets: two specialized agencies tasked with protecting physical or cybersonic zones against a shared adversary. Success in each stratum hinges on military resources; if the defending agency deploys more resources than the adversary at a specific target, that location remains secured, thereby incrementing their utility. Furthermore, the framework allows cooperative budget transfers contingent upon mutual advantage. We rigorously define the Stable Equilibrium of Subgames for the SCDG, encompassing tactics for lateral agency resource sharing and adversarial budget planning. Empirical and comparative analysis illustrates that adherence to this equilibrium maximizes secured targets, validating the SCDG as a robust methodology for modeling critical interdisciplinary resource management under simultaneous multi-level insurgencies.

Speech sounds occupy a complex, multidimensional perceptual space with nuanced variations. Identifying distinct speech categories is cognitively difficult and exhibits substantial variation among individuals as well as across populations. Despite its importance, the neural mechanisms explaining these cross-subject and cross-language differences remain poorly understood. Traditional research has often resorting either to pooled analyses that overlook individual variability or separate analyses that obscure human commonalities, making neither approach suitable for valid cross-population and cross-subject comparisons. To address this limitation, we propose a new Bayesian mixed multidimensional scaling technique designed to capture heterogeneity between different subject groups. A Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm is implemented for fitting the model's posteriors, and the method's efficacy is tested via synthetic data. When applied to an auditory neuroscience study of specific interest, the framework reveals new insights into how lower-dimensional, biologically plausible latent structures explain stimulus distances and how these vary based on individual traits and linguistic background. Local Differential Privacy (LDP), a pivotal component in privacy-preserving data analysis in recent times, remains hindered by significant obstacles to broad implementation. Incorporating the distinct electromagnetic attributes of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) into deep neural networks is crucial for boosting both the explainability and physical interpretability of AI models. This study introduces Physics Guided Injected Learning (PGIL), a novel physically explicable convolutional neural network designed for SAR image classification. This framework consists of three components: (1) explainable modules that integrate prior physics insights, (2) a physics-guided layer to encode knowledge as physical-aware features, and (3) a physics-injecting module to adaptively merge these features into the classification workflow. Evaluation is conducted using a newly defined hybrid Image-Physics dataset derived from Sentinel-1 and Gaofen-3 SAR imagettes. Experimental outcomes reveal that PGIL significantly outperforms traditional data-driven convolutional networks and various pre-training approaches, specifically in scenarios constrained by limited labeled data. Furthermore, detailed analysis of the generated physical explanations highlights both model interpretability and the maintenance of prediction consistency with physical laws. Ultimately, this research advocates the proposed methodology's potential to advance the domain of physically explicable deep learning for SAR image analysis.

Integrating multi-spectral satellite observations with machine learning has been proposed as an avenue for tracking oceanic plastic pollution. Accordingly, this research presents a three-part contribution: first developing machine models for plastic detection; secondly introducing MAP-Mapper as an automated software tool for mapping plastic density; and third, scientifically appraising this entire methodology against realistic out-of-distribution challenges. The findings demonstrate that leveraging high-precision models is paramount in reducing false positive impacts regarding subsequent analysis based on the spatial plastic abundance map. The constructed architectures enable user control between two configurations: MAP-Mapper-High precision (abbreviated HP) to minimize error rates or MAP-Mapper-Bold/Optimal (abbreviated Opt), which prioritizes recall. The primary component, MAP-Mapper-High precision (HP model), notably elevated detection accuracy to 95\%, and achieved a balance of 87–83 precision and 70–81 recall. This study presents findings related to numerical analysis and the stability conditions of an explicit finite difference scheme applied to a comprehensive two-factor corporate bond framework. Counterfactual Thinking has emerged as a prominent paradigm in Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) because humans naturally grasp this line of reasoning. Consequently, we present a novel explanatory approach termed Alterfactual Explanations. We assess our approach through an extensive user study, demonstrating its capability to substantially improve participants' comprehension of AI systems and showing that alterfactual explanations offer distinct advantages in conveying aspects of AI reasoning different from traditional methods.

Although significant advancements have been made in practical asynchronous Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) consensus protocols, current best-in-class designs continue to exhibit suboptimal performance. To achieve maximum throughput, many existing linear-amortized protocols compel participating nodes to broadcast massive transaction batches, severely compromising latency. Additionally, the broadcast data from up to $f$ slowest nodes might be ignored before consensus is reached, effectively censoring them; however, implementing defenses such as computationally expensive threshold cryptography or accepting expanded communication overhead introduces further efficiency penalties. We introduce Dumbo-NG, a new form of asynchronous BFT atomic broadcast designed to overcome these unresolved challenges. At its core is an intricate direct reduction from asynchronous atomic broadcast to multi-value Byzantine Agreement (MValBA) that ensures a quality property. Our protocol structure uniquely enables fully concurrent transaction dissemination and the asynchronous agreement process. Yielding two key advantages, it resolves the trade-off between throughput and latency by achieving near-maximal throughput with negligible latency increases, and all transactions broadcast by any honest node are guaranteed to eventually be included, neutralizing the risk of censorship without additional costs. We implemented Dumbo-NG and evaluated it against leading censorship-resistant asynchronous BFT systems, including Speeding-Dumbo and the enhanced variant of the DispersedLedger known as sDumbo-Dl, before performing a rigorous performance comparison. Long-document retrieval (L-DR) presents substantial difficulties for reading comprehension and information retrieval, yet pre-training models have recently shown promise in the retrieval and ranking stages for such documents despite lingering challenges like noisy labels, suboptimal document representations, and biased negative sampling. To address data noise and achieve balanced long document retrieval, we introduce a "bag" sampling strategy combined with a group-wise Local Contrastive Learning (LCL) method. Specifically, we utilize head-mixed-tail passage sequences to represent long documents, employ dense retrieval to generate candidate sets in the retrieval phase, and then divide retrieval data into distinct bags during ranker optimization to select negatives locally within each bag. This approach combines two objective functions: standard loss and a custom LCL-based framework tailored for the group-specific bag sampling. Within this second framework, following the encoding of queries and documents, we extract global bag-level features using convolutional operations and max-pooling. This enhancement improves the system's robustness regardless of label noise and facilitates the calculation of group-oriented LCL losses. Experimental results on the MS MARCO Long document retrieval dataset demonstrate that our model outperforms existing entries on the leaderboard.

Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding (L-MAPF) involves guiding a team of agents through various tasks on a shared graph, requiring visits to multiple locations while preventing inter-agent collisions. Standard L-MAPF strategies typically decompose this into a sequence of similar, single-shot "MAPF" queries using the Rolling-Horizon Collision Resolution (RHCR) approach. In this framework, the outcome of one query influences subsequent ones by creating similar start and target configurations as well as recurring collision scenarios, suggesting that past solutions could expedite the handling of future queries. However, existing L-MAPF planners process these consecutive queries independently without leveraging prior knowledge. Addressing this limitation, we propose exRHCR, a novel RHCR-based methodology that actively utilizes historical query data. Specifically, we adapt Priority-Based Search (PBS)—an established state-of-the-art MAPF solver—to its enhanced variant, called PBS, which enables the use of precedence information (agent priorities) generated by previous MAPF instances as an initialization boost to accelerate the new search. Empirical analysis shows that exRHCR outperforms RHCR by up to 39% in speed and holds significant promise for boosting system throughput by allowing the handling of more agents within defined execution timeframes when resolving task sequences in L-MAPF environments.

Achieving precise segmentation of Anatomical Brain Barriers to Cancer spread (ABCs) is essential for the automated delineation of Clinical Target Volumes (CTV) for brain tumors in radiotherapy treatment. Although U-Net architectures represent state-of-the-art segmentation, they often struggle with ABCs due to their diverse shapes and sizes, particularly in capturing thin structures like the falx cerebri that appear across only a limited number of slices. To address these challenges, we introduce the High and Multi-Resolution Network (HMRNet), composed of high-resolution and multi-scale branches that combine robust structural representation with fine contextual detail. We also incorporate a Bidirectional Feature Calibration (BFC) module, allowing the two branches to mutually refine spatial feature maps. To manage varying object positions and scales, the network operates on a post-localization input to ensure refined segmentation. Examinations on the MICCAI 2020 ABCs challenge dataset demonstrate three primary findings: our two-stage approach outperforms single-stage methods, the dual-branch structure effectively enhances performance on small and slender anatomical features by preserving high resolution, and the BFC block surpasses unidirectional attention techniques. Ultimately, our model secured second place in the 2020 ABCs challenge and offers greater precision for defining the CTV in radiotherapy planning.

We present findings on the detection of a highly eccentric, long-period Jovian planet around the hot Jupiter HD 83443. Synthesizing radial velocity observations acquired by four distinct instruments—AAT/UCLES, Keck/HIRES, HARPS, and Minerva-Australis—for over twenty years, our analysis confirms the existence of an orbiting planet with a minimum mass (m sin i) of $1.35^{+0.07}_{-0.06}\,M_J$. This body traverses an orbit characterized by a semi-major axis $a$ of $8.0\pm0.8$\,au and high eccentricity (e = $0.76\pm0.05). By integrating these velocity results with proper-motion anomalies from \textit{Gaia} eDR3 and \textit{Hipparcos}, we estimate the planet's dynamical mass to be between $0.87$ and $2.0\,M_J$ ($1.5^{+0.5}_{-0.2} M_{\rm Jupt}$). Rigorous dynamical simulations identify stable zones around the system capable of housing further planetary bodies, notably regions existing within the host star's habitable circle. HD 83443 represents a distinct system housing both a close-orbiting hot Jupiter and an external companion. The extreme orbital eccentricity implies recent dynamical interactions that relocated the hot Jupiter inward while propelling the outer body onto its expansive, tilted trajectory, suggesting previous gravitational scattering was responsible.

Although existing template- and learning-driven Automated Program Repair (APR) tools identified patches for numerous benchmark defects, an analysis reveals that they struggle significantly with omission faults. Specifically, template-based methods cannot identify insertion points without an existing location to attach a template, while learning-based methods modeling repair as Neural Machine Translation (NMT) lack faulty code to translate. To overcome this limitation, we introduce GLAD, a novel generative learning approach specialized in synthesizing if-clauses. Distinctive from traditional NMT repair techniques that require error location to translate, GLAD leverages Language Models which facilitate the generation of missing code entirely from type constraints. By applying a context-sensitive grammar for generation, it narrows the search space intelligently, while dynamic debugging is employed for efficient candidate ranking, significantly reducing verification expenses. Due to this shift from translation to synthesis, GLAD offers novel capabilities complementary to current tools: it successfully corrects 16 specific faults from Defects4J v1.2 for N and Java classes, where applicable NMT-based methods previously failed, while maintaining efficiency not seen in current tools. An assessment of these resolutions shows GLAD rapidly devises complex expressions that challenge standard APR techniques.

Dynamics in complex systems are often modeled as node interactions over an imposed network; yet, inferring this coupled interaction structure and node dynamics solely from temporal data of node states remains a challenging problem. Traditional approaches address either network structure identification or dynamic reconstruction independently, failing to perform well on both simultaneously. This paper introduces an integrated framework designed to recover both network topology and node dynamics concurrently from observed time-series data. By employing a Bernoulli sampling mechanism differentiable with respect to parameters to hypothesize connectivity, and utilizing neural networks to govern state evolution based on these hypotheses, we optimize all parameters via stochastic gradient descent to maximize a data likelihood function. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high-precision reconstruction of both elements for a variety of scenarios. Furthermore, it handles binary, discrete, and continuous sequences robustly, maintaining performance even in the presence of noise and missing data.

While companies commonly enforce management hierarchies in workers to enable collaboration, decision-making, and oversight, the day-to-day patterns of employee interaction tend to evolve naturally based on both these managerial ties and the entity's operational necessities. Researchers in organizational management suggest links between hierarchical frameworks (organizational trees) and communication dynamics affecting business outcomes; concurrently, network scientists analyze the topological makeup of communication flows across varied corporate structures. Yet, the specific nexus connecting formal architecture to spontaneous communication among staffers remains ambiguous. Our research investigates correlations between organizational hierarchy and message patterns across roughly 200,000 staff members at a major technology firm in May 2019. To capture message frequency moving vertically and horizontally through the chain of command, we introduce novel metrics regarding reciprocity and shortest-path distances in trees. By splitting the corporation into 88 teams, conceptualized as organizational trees anchored by senior leadership, our study isolates distinct communication architectures both within and across units. These architectures correlate with functional areas such as engineering, marketing, sales, and research. Finally, we examine the connection between routine interstaff communications and supervisory levels within the specific company, offering empirical tests against established theories concerning organizational performance and behavior.

Graph Neural Networks have recently set new standards for semi-supervised node classification, yet their adaptation to environments with merely a handful of labels remains insufficiently explored. Pseudo-labeling, a common semi-supervised strategy, aims to overcome data scarcity by augmenting training sets with unlabeled nodes predicted with high certainty within a cyclic learning framework. Existing approaches frequently encounter two critical issues: first, their overly conservative reliance on high confidence often results in redundant node selection, providing limited incremental value during supervised re-training because such nodes mirror existing labeled data. Secondly, these methods wrongly apply identical loss functions to both pseudo-labels and authentic labels, thereby neglecting their disparate utility for classification tasks. To address these challenges, this paper introduces InfoGNN, a novel framework designed to enable effective training of GNNs with extreme label scarcity. Our core methodology involves selecting the most informative nodes through mutual information maximization, ensuring they best encapsulate local neighborhood characteristics. Comprehensive evaluations across six real-world graph datasets reveal that InfoGNN substantially outperforms both current state-of-the-art and robust self-supervised alternatives on graphs.

Three-level $\Lambda$ systems are fundamental to many quantum information architectures where the auxiliary excited state mediates logical evolution between lower qubit states. Nevertheless, these higher levels can introduce undesirable non-rotational couplings that drive leakage and other decoherence processes, significantly hindering gate accuracy. This work addresses this issue by utilizing coherent population trapping within a gate-implementation protocol and developing control strategies to mitigate off-resonant interactions, thereby boosting fidelity by multiple orders of magnitude. For a specific coupling configuration, we identify an precise solution that yields perfectly accurate gating through static frequency shifts. In broader scenarios, we enhance operation precision by applying corrective pulse modulations that extend rapid adiabatic gate (DRAG) techniques to three-level $\Lambda$ systems. These approaches facilitate rapid, high-quality quantum gates across diverse optical quantum hardware, including trapped ions, color centers, and semiconductor quantum dots.

Few-shot learning addresses a critical hurdle in machine learning by mitigating the excessive time and resources required to construct vast labeled datasets. However, prevailing approaches typically face two distinct drawbacks: they either depend on complex model architectures and loss functions that limit interpretability or rely on statistical techniques based on assumptions that frequently fail across varied datasets. Expanding upon recent advancements that infer small-sample class distributions from more compatible larger classes, we introduce a Generalized sampling method designed to approximate few-shot distributions for classification by converting all large classes into weighted random variables. Additionally, we implement covariance shrinkage to enhance stability when encountering singular covariances caused by overparameterized features or limited data volume. Empirically, our sampled data points effectively approximate target few-shot classes, even when no similarity exists with larger classes in the training pool. Notably, our framework functions seamlessly with any standard off-the-shelf feature extractor and achieves superior performance on miniImageNet, CUB, and Stanford Dogs benchmarks, improving upon state-of-the-art methods by 3–5% on both 5-way-1shot and 5-way-5-shot tasks, as well as gaining 1% accuracy on demanding cross-domain evaluations.

Computer vision and machine learning technologies provide innovative approaches for the automatic classification and analysis of data stemming from complex simulations. We present a robust ensemble machine learning framework designed to independently categorize and analyze the output of simulators, specifically targeting distinct structure catalogs within turbulent flows. Using an unsupervised clustering algorithm, physical structures in simulation imagery are segmented by grouping similar pixels. To ensure the accuracy and resilience of these segmented region edges, data from multiple simultaneously evaluated clustering tasks are combined via stackable image mask integration. This Statistical Combined Ensemble (SCE) of cluster masks generates cluster reliability metrics for both individual pixels and associated segments entirely without requiring prior human input. Additionally, optimizing the number of clusters necessary for data description is achievable through the comparison of cluster similarity across ensemble variations. Crucially, relying on ensemble-averaged spatial boundaries, the SCE approach constructs more accurate and stable boundaries of Regions of Interest (ROI) for distinct image datasets. We utilize this algorithm on 2D simulation snapshots representing magnetically dominated, fully-kinetic turbulent plasma flows, a context demanding precise ROI definition to measure intermittent phenomena identified as current sheets geometrically.

Finally, simulations demonstrate the efficacy of this preconditioning approach in minimizing coherence and improving sparse signal recovery.

Fekete polynomials assign to each prime number $p$ a polynomial having $-1$ or $1$ coefficients for all non-constant terms, while the constant term remains $0$; these coefficients encode the pattern of quadratic residues modulo $p$. Originally investigated in the 19th century in connection with Dirichlet $L$-functions, our paper introduces two closely related polynomials. We then express their special values at various integers using class numbers and generalized Bernoulli numbers. Furthermore, we analyze the Galois group and splitting fields associated with these polynomials, specifically proposing a conjecture regarding the structure of these Galois groups.

We introduce an approach to greatly improve the strong coupling rate for the interaction between photons within an optical cavity and individual quantum emitters (such as trapped ions, quantum dots, or atoms). We demonstrate that employing specifically tailored non-spherical mirrors enables the existence of resonator eigenmodes featuring substantial field concentration at their core. Configurations produce considerably lower beam spreading compared to near-concentric spherical-mirror cavities, a reduction that translates to minimized round-trip losses and elevated cooperativity. Our concepts have been validated through the application of mode-matching analysis, accompanied by an examination of their stability against various potential manufacturing imperfections.

Recently introduced "plug-and-play" (PnP) image recovery methods for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have achieved impressive results. While these algorithms follow designs similar to conventional iterative frameworks like ADMM, FISTA, or primal-dual splitting (PDS), the key distinction lies in replacing the proximal update step with an execution of a task-tailored denoiser—such as BM3D or DCon. However, the convergence of PnP methods relies heavily on an algorithmic stepsize parameter that must be manually calibrated for peak efficacy. We present a swift and resilient auto-tuning variant specifically designed for the PnP-PDS method, leveraging precise estimation of measurement-noise variance derived from initial MRI scans. Our experiments demonstrate rapid convergence to performance near that of an ideal, expertly tuned approach, significantly outperforming prior autopilot strategies.

We introduce the Mock Lenses in Time (MOLET) package, a flexible and self-consistent forward modelling tool capable of generating pixel-scale and time-series simulations for strongly variable systems with time-varying gravitational lenses. While prior methods often ignored the time dimension, MOLET explicitly incorporates diverse variability mechanisms such as microlensing, a feature directly linked to time delay, H0, measurements, and predictions regarding caustic crossings. Given that time-domain experiments have gained popularity through recent surveys and benefit from a rigorous, model-aware quantification of statistical and systematic errors for improved accuracy, we apply MOLET to analyze how measuring delays in lensed quasars and supernovae varies across multiple wavelengths and depends on differing assumptions about both intrinsic evolution and microlensing. This initial assessment highlights that observing cadences and multi-wavelength synthesis are crucial factors when correctly recovering delays. The MOLET source code is accessible from \texttt{\url{https://github.com/gvernard/molet}}.

Multiplying large-integers polynomials remains a critical bottleneck in most public-key cryptography systems, affecting everything from elliptic-curve cryptography to currently researched post-quantum algorithms. This paper introduces a comprehensive suite of large-interval polynomial multipliers, designed specifically for use in hardware cryptocores to address these multiplication challenges. The library offers both digitized and non-digitized multiplier implementations, allowing circuit engineers flexibility during the creation of designs, while supporting C++ generators that synthesize this architecture automatically into FPGA/ASIC-ready Verilog logic and ASIC-tuned synthesis frameworks. Furthermore, the generator facilitates simultaneous rapid prototyping of numerous architectures, making the otherwise difficult optimization and exploration process of the complex search space related to polynomial multiplication a significantly more intuitive and straightforward design step.

The widespread application of artificial neural networks (ANNs), now ubiquitous in various scientific computing fields, rapidly escalates the energy consumption of modern high-performance systems. A promising, potentially more sustainable alternative involves innovative neuromorphic architectures that execute ANNs directly in hardware; however, evidence of actual efficiency gains for scientific applications has been scarce. In this study, we introduce a methodology for quantifying energy consumption and computation time for ANN inference using standard hardware. Furthermore, we developed a target architecture and projected these metrics based on a leading-state-of-the-art analog in-memory computing (AIMC) framework, a cornerstone of emerging neuromorphic technology. Our comparative analysis examines specific use cases in two-dimensional condensed matter systems—specifically quantum many-body problems—and at 40 MHz detection frequencies via particle physics at the Large Hadron Collider. Our findings reveal that AIMC platforms can reduce computation times by up to tenfold while consuming energy three orders of magnitude less than conventional hardware, highlighting the significant promise of neuromorphic systems to accelerate and debottleneck scientific computing sustainability.

A key aspect of our approach involves fusing 3D detections from multiple viewpoints prior to the association step; this strategy significantly reduces identity switches and refines motion modeling. Experiments conducted on large-scale driving datasets demonstrate that this "fuse before associate" method offers a substantial performance boost compared to post-hoc fusion. On the rigorous NuScenes 3D tracking benchmark, our method establishes a new state-of-the-art, achieving a 12.6% improvement in Average Multijob Object Trajectory Association (AMOTA) relative to the existing camera-based techniques, which represents a 6.5% gain over previous state-of-the-art results while utilizing an identical 3D object detector.

We present LIMES, a novel technique designed for learning from non-stationary streaming data, drawing inspiration from meta-learning achievements. Together, these enable an efficient learning process from varying streaming distributions that offers no additional trainable weights and minimal overhead in memory or compute compared to a standard single model. Empirical evaluations on Twitter datasets demonstrate that LI MES surpasses alternative approaches in accuracy.

This paper outlines the scientific motivations behind constructing Band 1 (35–52 GHz) receivers within ALMA's current Development Program. This expanded frequency range was selected specifically to maximize the scientific return of the facility. We focus initially on two primary drivers: the evolutionary processes of dust grains in protoplanetary and debris disks, and the behavior of molecular gas within galaxies throughout cosmic reionization. Addressing these topics using Band 1 will substantially enhance ALMA's primary science goals, while a wide array of additional line and continuum observations will leverage the facility's exceptional resolution and sensitivity. Specific targets include probing the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect in galaxy clusters; investigating Very Small and spinning dust; tracing ionized jets from young stars; and analyzing Sgr A* and its flaring activity. Other applications cover solar accelerator sites, pulsar wind nebulas, radio supernovae, and X-ray binaries. Furthermore, spectral observations will target chemical differentiation in cloud cores, complex carbon chain molecules and extragalactic recombination lines. We will utilize masers and Zeeman measurements to study magnetic fields, track molecular outflows from young stars, and explore the co-evolution of star formation with active galactic nuclei, specifically targeting galaxy molecular content at a redshift of z ~3. Over the 35–50 GHz range, ALMA offers comparable or superior sensitivity to the JVLA, with performance gains growing at higher frequencies. Additionally, despite smaller antennas and baselines, ALMA's greater baseline count and dedicated single-dish capabilities grant it distinct advantages for imaging extended emission, producing large mosaical fields, and achieving high-fidelity images essential for the outlined science goals.

Characterizing material loss in superconducting circuits necessitates reliable techniques for extracting the internal and coupling $Q$-factors (quality factors) of microwave resonators. While single-port, reflection-mode measurements remain standard—often dictated by device or experimental design—their accuracy in cryogenic setups hinges on calibration performed at millikelvin temperatures to compensate for impedance mismatches. This manuscript demonstrates a data-centric single-port calibration method, utilizing off-the-shelf microwave standards and a vector network analyzer mounted inside a dilution refrigerator to reach these ultra-low temperatures, thereby validating its utility for quantum experiments. Furthermore, to confirm reliability over reflections based measurements, these results for over-coupled two- and three-dimensional resonators are compared against established two-port transmission techniques.

Visual representations are characterized by the responses of neuron populations to images, which form what is termed a "tuning landscape" across the entire space of images. Understanding the specific structure of this landscape across high-dimensional dimensions is central to current inquiries. In our research, we employ the concepts of level sets and Morse theory to characterize these landscapes. Drawing upon previous in-vivo measurements of two-dimensional tuning maps across various neural regions, this study establishes a statistically robust signature for these maps by analyzing changes in their topologies. Our results reveal a gradual evolution of this topological signature across the cortical hierarchy, paralleling trends observed in units of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Furthermore, we investigated the geometry of level sets on CNN tuning landscapes, refining the idea that while higher-level units approximate locally as isotropic radial basis functions, this characterization does not hold globally. These findings demonstrate how level sets serve as a powerful tool for interpreting neuronal activation patterns within image spaces.

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) serves to prevent or treat malaria resulting from mosquito exposure; however, its proposed utility for COVID-19 treatment has lacked scientific validation, creating risks to public safety by skewing community perceptions as misinformation spreads through informal networks. An investigation of this period examines social network responses to recommendations supporting HCQ for COVID-19. Researchers analyzed over 164,000 tweets collected between February and December 2020, utilizing text mining to track opinion trajectories and behavioral shifts among platforms. Descriptive findings revealed erratic response patterns that closely followed social media coverage and news updates concerning HCQ and COVID-19 treatment developments. The research connected tweet content with Google search volumes to map regional viewpoints on HCQ efficacy across states and exposed a dramatic shift in overall public sentiment over the study period; while initial support was high, levels notably dropped by October. Furthermore, comparisons of automated analysis against a human-manually classified sample of 21.8 samples demonstrated that the Google Cloud Natural Language tool exceeded the performance of "Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner," achieving particular accuracy in categorizing sarcastic statements.

Compared to model-free approaches, model predictive control that relies on data benefits from enhanced sample efficiency due to model learning and scales effectively as the planning budget expands; however, it remains computationally burdensome for extended horizons and difficult to deploy with high-precision event modeling. We bridge these approaches by leveraging task-oriented latent dynamics models derived from learning. In our TD-MPC framework, local short-horizon trajectory optimization is driven by these dynamics models while long-term returns are approximated by terminal value functions; both components are acquired through joint temporal difference learning. Experiments demonstrate that TD-MPC outperforms existing methods in both imagery and state-space continuous control benchmarks within DMControl and Meta-World regarding sample efficiency and asymptotic performance. Resources including code and demonstration videos are accessible at https://nicklashansen.github.io/td-mpc.

New wireless applications require mathematical models and tools to systematically assess network reliability. This study introduces two metrics to evaluate wireless mesh routing: one for flooding and one for unicast routing. The Flooding Path Probability (FPP) assesses end-to-end packet delivery probability specifically for nodes that retransmit a packet only after all upstream neighbors have broadcast it. Conversely, the Unicast Retransmission Flow (URF) measure estimates delivery probability when relay nodes repeatedly forward a unicast packet until receiving an acknowledgement or attempting all available outgoing links. Unlike previous heuristics, both metrics rely on specific forwarding models to derive closed-form expressions of delivery probability from link-level statistics and network topology data. Furthermore, we present a distributed, greedy algorithm leveraging the URF metric to build robust topologies. This method generates a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) from a graph with edge weights corresponding to success probabilities, employing decreasing reliability threshold vectors to control node participation. Simulation results indicate that, on average, this approach constructs significantly more dependable structures than traditional minimum-hop DAG approaches.

Investigating the growth of galaxies and their star formation quenching, astronomers increasingly rely on the stellar surface density within the inner kiloparsec (\(\Sigma_{1}\)) as an index. Current models suggest that forming a dense central core might require a prior increase in stellar density, though the link between \(\Sigma_{1}\) variations and shifts in stellar velocity dispersion remains unclear. To address this, we utilized Sloan Digital Sky Survey images combined with kinematical data for 1599 nearby galaxies from the SAMI and MaNGA surveys to examine how \(\Sigma_{1}\) correlates with the stellar spin parameter \(\lambda_{re}\) (calculated within one effective radius). Findings on the star-forming main sequence—normalized at fixed stellar mass—reveal that \(\lambda_{re}\) evolves alongside \(\Sigma_{1}\); as main sequence galaxies form new stars, \(\Sigma_{1}\) grows while rotational support remains steady or marginally increases. Below this main sequence, however, these parameters diverge, with passive systems exhibiting less variation in central density but a broader diversity in stellar rotation. These trends imply that passive galaxies constitute a structurally varied population with multifaceted evolutionary histories compared to rotating star-formers. Finally, our results suggest that any substantial recent growth in dispersion-driven bulges at redshift \(z\sim0\) likely occurs concurrently with or shortly after galaxies have been quenched.
